speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on yesterday's order paper standing in my name there was a question, the pertinent part of which read as follows:
Has the appellant in income tax appeal board case No. 227-
I shall skip the unnecessary wording-
*-at any time had any contracts with the federal government, or any department or agency thereof?
My question of privilege relates to the fact that, as I see it, the answer is hardly adequate. The answer as found on page 451 of yesterday's Hansard says, in part:
...the minister who was a party to the proceedings had a check made as to whether at any time since the appellant company purchased the property referred to in the judgment, the federal government had awarded any contract of any kind to the appellant company or to its subsidiary referred to in the judgment.
As Your Honour will notice, I asked whether there had been any contracts awarded to this company at any time. The answer given is that there have not been any since the time the property referred to in the judgment was purchased. Obviously this leaves an inference which can be drawn one way or another as to what happened prior to the time that property was purchased.
Then further, on my question of privilege, I would like to point out that the judgment referred to indicated that this property, up to that time, had not been purchased at all. It had only been leased with the option of purchase. That makes the phrase "since the time the property was purchased" meaningless.
In the light of these facts I would hope that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) might consider bringing down a more complete answer to my question.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I understand him to say that he would make a statement on the situation today with respect to Formosa. In view of the anxiety that is felt by many people in this country regarding the statements of policy made yesterday by the President of the United States, can the minister tell us whether the United States has been informed that Canada's policy remains as it was, and that we are not entangled in any of these Formosan adventures?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to what my hon. friend has said, and also in reply to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), I shall make a statement on this matter now, as follows:
The President of the United States yesterday sent to congress an important message dealing with the situation in the Formosa straits. The President's proposals in this message are, of course, a matter of United States policy. The United States has particular commitments of its own in this area. These, and the effect of the President's message on them, will now be under consideration by congress and it would not, of course, be appropriate for me, or for any member of this government, to comment on this aspect of the matter.
Although we are not involved in United States commitments in this area, we are of course deeply concerned over the dangerous situation existing there and we, with other free governments, are anxious that steps should be taken to bring to an end the fighting which has now been taking place for some time along the China coast.


In this message the President of the United States referred to the possibility of action by the United Nations to bring about a ceasefire. The United Nations has, in Indonesia, Palestine and in other parts of the world, been successful in bringing to an end fighting which might have had dangerous consequences, and if it could achieve similar results in this case it would be a cause, I am sure, of great satisfaction to us all.
If the question is raised in the United Nations-and there are reports that it will soon be raised-this would presumably take place in the security council of which Canada is not at present a member. However, we are being kept informed of developments in regard to the possibility of such a reference, and we are watching the matter with great interest and some concern. Incidentally, an essential party to any ceasefire of this kind would be the communist government of China, which, though a nonmember of the United Nations, would have to be invited, I assume, to participate in the security council deliberations if they were to have any chance of success. Whether this particular government would accept such an invitation is another matter.
While it is not proper for me to comment on United States policy in this matter which is now being considered by congress, I think I can say that any move or proposal within the United Nations or through diplomatic channels which could serve to achieve the purpose as stated in the President's message "to improve the prospects of peace in the area" will be warmly welcomed by the parliament and by the people of this country.
Before the Korean armistice I expressed on more than one occasion in this house the view of the Canadian government that Formosa should be neutralized as far as possible while hostilities continued in Korea. We thought then, and we think now, that the final disposition of Formosa should be a subject to be discussed at a conference on Far Eastern problems which at that time we thought might be held after the cessation of fighting in Korea. That was the view adopted by the political committee of the United Nations general assembly on January 13,	1951.
Despite developments since then, it remains the view of the government that the final disposition of Formosa should be dealt with by international negotiation, at a conference, if you like, on Far Eastern problems, if one could be held. Certainly, in any decision regarding the future of Formosa the wishes of the people there, which are often forgotten in discussions of this matter, should be a primary consideration. Pending such a decision I think that a strong case can be

made for the neutralization of Formosa both in order to prevent any assault upon it by communist forces and also so that it will not be used as a base for invasion of the mainland.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: The President did not say that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
In this area of tension and danger a distinction can validly be made between the position of Formosa and the Pescadores and the islands off the China coast now in nationalist hands. The latter are indisputably part of the territory of China; the former, Formosa and the Pescadores, which were Japanese colonies for fifty years prior to 1945 and had had a checkered history before that, are not. I suggest therefore that the considerations which recommend the neutralization of Formosa and the Pescadores do not necessarily apply to the coastal islands so close to the mainland and a hundred miles or so away from Formosa. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I welcome that part of the President's message which looks to the redeployment of the nationalist forces which are now in these islands. "Some of these forces", the President's message states, "are scattered throughout smaller off-shore islands as a result of historical rather than military reasons directly related to defending Formosa."
My understanding of the basis of a truce or cease-fire is that neither the nationalists, the government of China which we recognize, nor the communists need be asked to give up their claims on the territory now held by the other side. What they would be asked to give up of course is the use of military means to achieve their aspirations. In other words, negotiations for a cease-fire need not involve any question of the final disposition of the territory in dispute; for in our view this is a suitable matter for international negotiation at a later date through the United Nations or otherwise.
I am sure this house will particularly welcome the closing paragraph of the President's message which is as follows:
Our purpose is peace. That cause will be served if we demonstrate our unity and our determination. In all that we do we shall remain faithful to our obligations as a member of the United Nations to be ready to settle our international disputes by peaceful means in such a manner that international peace and security, and justice, are not endangered.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon.
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked the following question:
Is the minister aware of the steps being taken by the Canadian National Railways to move the foundry from the Transcona shops, at Winnipeg, to Montreal? In view of what this means to the employees affected, and in view of the central location of the Transcona shops, in Canada, will the minister ask the Canadian National to reconsider this move?
I have spoken to the management of the Canadian National Railways and they inform me that their dieselization program has now progressed to the point where there is insufficient casting work to justify the operation of two foundries.
At Point St. Charles the Canadian National has a modern foundry, the only one properly equipped for major casting work such as steam locomotive cylinders. The decision reached therefore, in the interests of economic operation, is that casting work should be consolidated at Point St. Charles and operations at the Transcona foundry discontinued.
I might add that there are 22 men now employed at the Transcona foundry. The transfer of work to Point St. Charles foundry will necessitate an adjustment in staff and 12 of these men will, in accordance with the provisions of the governing wage agreement, be given the opportunity of transferring to Point St. Charles.

The house resumed, from Monday, January 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by inexorable logic this house is moving to a momentous decision after what may go down in the records of the Canadian parliament as an historic debate maintained on a level worthy of the occasion.
There have been some truly remarkable contributions to this debate. One thinks of the illuminating and authoritative pronouncement made on the subject of German rearmament by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes). One admires the courageous stand taken in this house by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). One can admire courage wherever one finds it. One can commend as well statesmanlike utterances such as those the house has heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and others.
It was necessary that speeches of this quality should be made in this house on this occasion. The pity is that the country had not heard at an earlier date as authoritative and illuminating pronouncements from the government as those made in this debate by at least two government ministers. More than in any other aspect of public affairs it is in the field of our external affairs that the people need a lead from the government and from parliament, because so many of the decisions are arrived at in secret negotiations. We have
North Atlantic Treaty
seen in the vacuum of silence left by the government over the past several months the inevitable result: where ignorance and misunderstanding abound there is fertile soil for communist propaganda.
I say, therefore, that it is regrettable that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not make this same speech or similar speeches on a dozen earlier occasions in different parts of Canada. I wish the Prime Minister had delivered such speeches. Indeed I wish the government, when they decided not to call parliament at an earlier date, had undertaken to campaign across Canada for the purpose of bringing these necessary facts before the Canadian people. Therefore, while this debate in the house has now reached its fourth day, it has nevertheless furthered a vitally important purpose in bringing to the attention of the Canadian people important and inescapable considerations which bear upon the decision that is now to be taken in their name.
Events have been moving swiftly in the past twelve months. Who among us ten years ago could have foreseen that the House of Commons today would be on the point of taking a decision, not only on German rearmament but in relation to the association of Germany with the western world, ourselves included, in an alliance? This is one of the strange contradictions of history. It would have been different indeed had the Russians proved themselves trustworthy since the war. They are responsible by their aggression and by their duplicity for the fact that we are now taking the course that has been presented to us, a course which they condemn and seek by every means at their disposal to thwart.
We need look back no farther than last spring to the negotiations at Geneva when the western nations, and France in particular, were required to negotiate from weakness. And while at Geneva the best was done that could have been done in salvaging a virtually impossible situation, I hope that we in this house have decided we do not wish to face any more situations where we must attempt to grasp peace out of virtual defeat and weakness.
Few could have foreseen after EDC had been defeated in the French national assembly last summer that there would have been raised up in its place a new form of agreement which is now on the point of being carried to a decision.
During these post-war years, ever since the Russians embarked upon their program of conquest and aggression, the greatest danger to the free world has lain in Europe. I for one will not forget my visit to the Canadian

North Atlantic Treaty
infantry brigade at Hanover in the fall of 1952, and I recall that Canadian troops and the nearest Russian troops were just 45 minutes' travel by road apart.
If this greatest danger has receded in the past year or two, that recession is due to our growing strength in that part of the world, but the danger remains and unless we of the free world greatly strengthen ourselves in the west we will continue also to be weak in the east in the face of the continued probing by the communists for and exploitation of our weak spots in that part of the world. None know this better than the Russians themselves, as is evidenced by their frantic efforts to prevent, thwart, defeat, or delay, by every kind of pressure at their disposal, the decision we are now about to take.
It is regrettable, sir, and I am sure surprising, that in this house there should have been put forward by a particular group of hon. members of this house that formidable array of decoys which the communists and those who have been listening to them have been offering to the Canadian public. These have been reviewed and I do not intend to dwell upon them. But let me just mention them in passing.
First, there is negotiation, the idea of "another conference", another conference wherein the Russians, of course, hope again to divide the west. But the decision we are taking does not preclude further negotiations, if the Russians want them. But when these negotiations are held they should on the part of the west be negotiations from strength and not from weakness. That surely is the lesson of Geneva of last spring.
The next is the decoy of coexistence. But the purpose of this measure is defensive. There is nothing in it to prevent peaceful coexistence.
Third, there is the decoy of Russian reasonableness. But if the Russians truly mean to be reasonable, and really mean to turn over a new leaf by co-operating, there is nothing in the decision we are about to take that prevents them from being reasonable and more reasonable than ever before.
The fourth decoy, and it is as dangerous as any, was uttered with some feeling in this house two days ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It was the plea that we should not take the decision at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, time is running against the west. It has been running against the west for a considerable period, and time is the one thing that we cannot afford to give at this stage in any further measure to the Russians.
Then there is the fifth decoy, that we must not provoke the Russians because they may increase their arms. Well, sir, that is just

the old form of naked appeasement rearing its ugly head again. If that argument had been followed there would today be no NATO in the world, and we should not forget that the Russians have done their very utmost at all stages to defeat NATO.
The sixth decoy is that this measure is going to prevent German unification on some sound basis. But there is nothing here that will prevent German unification on any sound basis. There is, however, much here that would prevent unification of Germany on the tyrannical terms that Russia would impose.
I may sum up my view, and I believe the view of most Canadians in relation to these decoys, in saying that we do not trust communists. Have we forgotten Korea? Have we forgotten Czechoslovakia? Are we forgetting what is happening in Indo-China today in those areas that have fallen within the sweep of communist rule? No! There is one man who knew the Russians much better evidently than some C.C.F. members in this house know them, and that is Karl Marx, who said, in an historic utterance:	"The Russian
bear is certainly capable of anything-as long as he knows the other animals he has to deal with are capable of nothing."
Then on the other side of the debate there are those facts which have been overlooked by those members of the C.C.F. who oppose the resolution. The first of these is the existence in fact of a divided Germany. Second is the fact that Eastern Germany is armed. I have seen the military police, the barrack police, on the other side of the iron curtain. The existence of an armed Eastern Germany under Russian control is a fact, and Russia means to stay in East Germany until she has fastened her system, as she hopes, for all time upon the necks of the people of East Germany.
Third, rearmament is not the equivalent of war. Members of the C.C.F. in this house have treated rearmament as though it were the equivalent of war. That has been one of the hopeless contradictions obsessing those who have raised their voices in opposition to the resolution.
As we see it, rearmament in the view taken by this Canadian parliament in these momentous recent years has been a guarantee against the outbreak of war. We deplore that it should be necessary to lay upon the Canadian people the burden of sustaining rearmament. But, sir, when we talk about welfare let us remember that the first duty we owe to the Canadian people in ministering to and preserving their welfare is to make sure that Canada as part of the western world does not become a victim of aggression.
The fourth factor is that the guarantees have been overlooked, and if there are those

who are disposed to regard those guarantees as insufficiently strong, let us remember that they are just as strong as are guarantees in the United Nations or guarantees in NATO, because in every instance those guarantees rest upon the pledges of a nation through its accredited representatives and no more.
Fifth, the fact has been overlooked that this is a purely defensive arrangement. A great injustice has been done by the evidently innocent misrepresentation of this fact in this house by C.C.F. members.
Sixth, and a vitally important consideration is this, that it is strength in this world in which we live which deters Russian aggression today. It is the possession by the United States in recent years of the atomic bomb which has bought safety for the west. Those of us who were in Berlin in the fall of 1948 and flew in on the airlift can recall the events of those days when the Russians were attempting to drive the western powers out of Berlin. We should not forget, sir, that it was courage, firmness, and force on the part of Britain and the United States in that situation that marked the turning point in the course of events in these post-war years. At that point had Britain, France and the United States shown weakness in the face of Russian strength and determination the whole course of subsequent events would have been changed. But Britain and the United States stood firm and made it quite clear that they would resist the land blockade. They set up that marvel of organization, the airlift; and from that time, as a result of that stand, the smaller nations in western Europe realized that they could safely commit their lot to the western nations and could join hands with them. It was out of that firm stand that NATO was born and became possible. Let us not forget that the only god the Russians know or respect is the god who is on the side of the big battalions, to use Napoleon's expression. We do not put ourselves in that category, but we know that these Russians respect strength and that it is strength we need if we wish to live in peace beside them.
The next fact overlooked is that the risks with regard to German rearmament have been exaggerated. At least we have these facts, Mr. Speaker, which are entitled to be given due weight. Atomic weapons will come into the hands of the Germans only by decision of the western powers, and their arms will be subject to inspection. Last night in this house from C.C.F. members we heard speeches that proceeded on the belief that Germany is still nazi and that the rearmament of Germany is equivalent to the resurrection of nazism and the nazi war machine. We are not going to forget the nazi atrocities. We are going to remember the way in which
North Atlantic Treaty
those nazi atrocities bathed Europe and far parts of the world in blood. But is there anyone here who seriously thinks that the nazis control the government of West Germany today? It is a fact that there is no stauncher democrat in all the world today than is Chancellor Adenauer. But on the other hand, in Eastern Germany there are nazis in high office.
Several nights ago we heard an authoritative pronouncement from the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) on the point of German rearmament. When it is said by C.C.F. members that the steps now being taken mean the resurrection of the nazi war machine, let us not overlook also some news items that have come to knowledge within recent days.
Here is a Reuters dispatch from Berlin of January 19:
The Russians have released former Field Marshal Ferdinand Schoerner, Hitler's war minister in the last days of world war II . . .
What has he been released for? Why is it that, as the news dispatch indicates, he has undertaken to send a letter of thanks to the Russians for his release? How does it happen that he is released at this particular time? And how does it happen that ViceAdmiral Voss was released by the Russians a few days ago? By the communists in Canada we have heard it charged that the purpose of releasing Kurt Meyer was so that he might lead some German army in the west. Yet we have a news dispatch of January 23 from Bonn which says as follows:
The wife of former German tank commander Maj. Gen. Kurt Meyer said her husband has no intention of accepting a communist offer to help build up East German armed forces.
Is there any greater duplicity we have seen in all of Russian chicanery, in all of communist propaganda, than to pretend that it was the intention of the western powers to make common cause with former nazi generals in order to build up a German army while at the same time the Russians were those who were fighting against the resurrection of the nazi war machine? This kind of authoritative information from Berlin and Bonn is surely the complete exposure of that type of Russian chicanery.
Let it be recognized that the lesson of destruction and devastation has not been lost entirely upon the Germans; that there will be on German soil the continued presence of British, French, United States and Canadian forces; that the German forces will be under the command of a NATO commander in chief; and that the Germans will simply not be strong enough, under the limitations that

North Atlantic Treaty
exist, to embark upon a war of aggression for unification of Germany. Yes, the western powers must and will remain there.
Mr. Speaker, I now put to the house the proposition that it is the duty of every member-particularly of those who have voiced opposition to it-to oppose this measure only on the assumption that if it lay within their power they would defeat it. It would be a betrayal of the responsibility that each member of this house owes to the house and to the Canadian people if he cast his vote against this measure while at the same time secretly hoping that the measure would be adopted or, knowing that the measure is going to be adopted, indulged in some irresponsible objections to it.
Mr. Speaker, the defeat of this measure- and it is this that the hon. members of the C.C.F. must be prepared to accept if they are taking a responsible course in this debate -would have results which would indeed be too dreadful to contemplate. It is true that the major risks lie in this direction. The first result would be international chaos.
The second would be such an outburst of Russian glee as would be suitable and appropriate only to a great communist triumph in the world. We would then indeed have played into the hands of the Russians and of the communist cause.
The third result would be that inevitable agonizing reappraisal on the part of the administration and congress at Washington of United States policy and the course that the United States is to follow in relation to Europe.
In the fourth place, for Germans it would mean an effective rebuff by the west to Adenauer and to German democracy. It would mean that we would be violating the promise that has been given to a democratic Germany, namely that we of the west are prepared to work with a democratic Germany. Chancellor Adenauer deserves the support of the west for he has taken the greatest of risks.
The fifth result would be in relation to France. It would inevitably mean the crash of the French government and such a period of instability in French government as we have not yet seen. The whole course of French history would indeed be in a precarious plight. The strength of the communists would be bound to upsurge in France.
In the sixth place, to what fate would Germany be consigned? The Russians want all of Germany, west as well as east, with them. Their blandishments and all their efforts have been directed towards that end these many years.

In the seventh place-and let us put this issue squarely before members of this house who have indicated their opposition to this resolution-we would have dealt a body blow, it may well be a fatal blow, to NATO itself. NATO is needed in the world today as much as it ever was needed. We know that the United Nations are not enough. They are not enough to guarantee peace. We recognized that when NATO was established with the aid of Canadian inspiration. NATO's existence is needed. NATO's very existence would be challenged by defeat of this measure.
In the eighth place, in our own land it would mean, on the part of the communists, that their frantic efforts had been crowned with success, and a new boost to the morale and the effrontery of communists in Canada.
So I say, with reluctance and regret, that those who in this debate have indicated their opposition to this measure have shown no realism; they have shown no competence to assume any governmental task. When it comes to comparing them with those of whom they profess to be the counterpart in other lands, may I say that they are indeed ideologically the followers not of Mr. Attlee but of Mr. Bevan. Appropriate indeed was the title applied to that group by the Montreal Gazette yesterday when they were heralded as "the Bevanly host". "Bevanly" indeed! Thank heaven they are not a host.
One may sympathize with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the C.C.F. party in the house, as he has had to submit to the humiliation of listening to the speeches that have been made by his followers in condemnation of the measure before us in this debate.
Sir, I think we must express surprise and at the same time regret that we should hear that the same organization, the C.C.F. national council, is about to sponsor a visit of Mr. Attlee to Canada. Let me make it clear, in relation to this news dispatch that reached us yesterday, that Mr. Attlee enjoys the respect of us all, whatever our political views may be. I am sure most members of the house have had the opportunity to meet Mr. Attlee, some of us on various occasions, and we all respect him. We respect and uphold the views that he expressed in support of this measure of German rearmament in the British House of Commons. Mr. Attlee will always be a welcome visitor to Canada, but, sir, it is something new for the leader of a political party in the United Kingdom to be coming to Canada on a visit sponsored by a Canadian political party. That is the news that came to us yesterday.

We are told that Mr. Attlee will make a coast to coast tour of Canada between April 11 and May 1 under the sponsorship of the C.C.F. national council. I am sure it would be regarded as effrontery if the Conservative party in this country invited Sir Winston Churchill or Sir Anthony Eden to come to Canada and undertake a tour under our auspices. It would inevitably be a political tour. Unquestionably use will be attempted to be made by the C.C.F. for their own political purposes of the forthcoming visit of Mr. Attlee which is to be sponsored by the C.C.F. national council.
If Mr. Attlee chooses to visit Russia or chooses to visit China on the invitation of the governments of those countries, I am sure it is no affair of ours, sir, but it is an affair of ours if the leader of a British political party comes to Canada to make a tour under the auspices of a Canadian political party. It seems to me, sir, while Mr. Attlee is widely respected by all of us here and will always be a welcome visitor to Canada, that he ought not to be accepting the sponsorship of a political party in Canada for his tour.
Finally, sir, I wish to say this about the course that we are taking. It is a momentous course, but I ask: Is it within the bounds of contemplation that Canada should follow a different course in this matter from that to which the British House of Commons has already committed Great Britain, that land which in its finest hour saved the world? Is it in this situation thinkable that Canada should follow a contrary course to that being followed by the United States which, whatever its faults and shortcomings may be. has at least taken the burden and responsibilities of world leadership in the post-war years? Is it thinkable that Canada should follow a different course from that to which the French national assembly has committed that nation, invaded three times in living memory, France which has bled? Is it thinkable, sir, is it within the realm of contemplation of hon. members of this house, that Canada should take a different course from that followed jointly by Britain, the United States, France and other western nations? I tell you if we were to take that different course this country would never again be able to lift up its head in international company, and that respect which Canada has won at international conferences over the years from the close of world war I to the present time would be lost forever.
There are dangers, yes. We are calculating those dangers, we are measuring and weighing them here and now; but is that any
North Atlantic Treaty
excuse for allowing ourselves to be paralysed by fear into insensibility and inaction? The western world has already suffered much by the fact that the communists have been outthinking and outplanning us. They have been planning ahead of us. We have been waiting always for them to take the lead and then we have been taking defensive measures to try to counteract those measures which they have taken in lead of us.
Sir, the measure now before us and the alliance to which it gives expression offer to us as part of the western world an opportunity, long sought and long awaited, to take the lead. The time has come indeed for bold and courageous measures. How often in this debate have I thought of those words of Shakespeare:
but I tell you, . . . out of this nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, safety.
There are dangers, but in accepting what dangers run with this decision we shall yet win safety. That is the lesson of the airlift. That is the lesson of these years. We cannot guarantee the result. It is an imperfect world. None, I am sure, is more conscious of the limitations of human wisdom than we who are about to vote on this measure today, but we must take the best advice and use the best sense we have. For my part, sir, I have no hesitation in following the course recommended by Churchill, Eden, Attlee, Eisenhower, Mendes-France and the great majority of the members of this house in preference to the course recommended and sought by Bevan, Malenkov and those members of the C.C.F. who have spoken against this measure.
This is the means by which we must seek to strengthen the European dikes against the tides of communist aggression if we would hope to have either strength or time to erect similar dikes in Asia or Africa.
My reasons for supporting this measure are not merely negative. They are positive. I do not accept the philosophy or view that the Germans can never change. I admit that there is much yet to be done to establish the contrary, but I am not prepared to accept a course that commits me for all time to the view that the Germans cannot change. I believe that there are great numbers of Germans who are anxious, in the spirit of democracy and in the spirit of freedom, to purge the stains that nazi brutality has left upon Germany and upon the world.
Nor can I accept the view that Germany and France are forever destined to be enemies. It may be, sir, that we are here witnessing the great fulfilment of a dream,

North Atlantic Treaty
more than we could ever have hoped for, a dream that was expressed by Sir Winston Churchill in these words but a few years ago:
If we could only weave Gaul and Teuton so closely together economically, socially and morally as to prevent the occasion of new quarrels, and make old antagonisms die in the realization of mutual prosperity and interdependence, Europe would rise again. It seemed to me that the supreme interest of the British people in Europe lay in the assuagement of the Franco-German feud, and that they had no other interests comparable or contrary to that.
In this land, where our ancestors are drawn alike principally from Anglo-Saxon and from French sources, surely we must echo that hope and share that dream. Are we not prepared to believe now as an act of faith that when Churchill uttered those words he spoke not simply for the living but also for those heroes who in a thousand military cemeteries people the sacred cities of the dead?

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel sure all hon. members will have heard with a great deal of apprehension the news reported in this morning's paper, that in the area of Formosa there is a situation which could readily explode into a new world war. I think that on this occasion it will be at least reassuring to the people of Canada that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, replying to the leader of this party, has stated the official position of Canada, indicating that the problem of Formosa should be settled by the United Nations, or over an arbitration table.
And so, in prefacing my remarks concerning the very serious situation facing us in connection with Formosa, I cannot but be astounded by the government's position when an attempt is made to solve a far less urgent problem, by means of an armaments race which, undoubtedly, will take place in connection with the matter before us. I refer of course to the agreement which would permit the entry of Germany into NATO, and involves the rearmament of Germany.
I do not intend to take much time answering some of the criticisms which have been made of members of this group who, like myself, hold the view that the rearming of Germany at this time is ill advised and fraught with many dangers.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who has just taken his seat took a great deal of time in his speech by innuendo and other references in an effort to indicate that the members of the C.C.F. are not sincere in their convictions. The hon. members for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) and Meadow Lake, did likewise. It is not my intention to take time to deal with these expressions. I am used to red baiting. I would say only

this, that it had never been the hallmark of Canadian democracy to have a slavish obedience to any political party or to any one idea. On the contrary the essence of parliamentary democracy in Canada is that any member can rise to his feet and express his opinion without fear of vilification.
And so today I intend to do just that. Each member who has spoken, whether in favour of the rearmament of Germany or otherwise, has expressed his fears as to the outcome of that decision. Each member, by one argument or another, has indicated that the proposal is fraught with many dangers and that a calculated risk is involved.
I believe it is ill advised and dangerous to the peace of the world to rearm Germany. One might very well argue emotionally about the atrocities committed under the nazi regime, but, in the light of the seriousness of the situation, I do not think we need do that. However, we must try to be realistic and objective in our approach to this great and complex problem.
The viewpoint expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs runs something like this: That there is a vacuum existing in Germany, and that unless the west moves to fill that vacuum, communism will move in. I do not agree with that, and I will support my contention with quotations. I shall quote first Dr. Russell who, in the issue of December 8, 1954, of The Nation has this to say:
The truth is so plain and simple that it seems as if governments must in time become aware of it: the communist and non-communist worlds can live together or die together. There is no other possibility. When both sides realize this, it may be hoped that they will choose to live rather than die.
And again, the well known writer George F. Kennan, former ambassador to the Soviet union, has this to say:
As many of you already know, I have never seen any evidence that the Soviet leaders have at any time since world war II (or before, for that matter) desired a general war between the Soviet union and the major capitalist powers, or looked to such a war as a likely means of achieving their objectives.
So I do not think there is any immediate concern in the matter of invasion of West Germany. As a matter of fact I believe that the rearming of West Germany can only mean that there will be reciprocation on the part of the Russians and that they, too, will increase their armaments to keep balance with those the west might provide for the Germans. Therefore I say the minister's argument that Russia will not take reciprocal action to keep her strength in armaments equal to that on the allied side is somewhat ridiculous.

Again, those who have supported the rearming of Germany have argued that, through strength, we can achieve the reunification of Germany. In this respect I believe that in rearming West Germany a curtain will be erected so that it will be very difficult to bring about any form of disarmament. And I believe there will be other dangers, one of which is that, in time, the German army, rearmed and under old nazi leaders and under the military control of the whole country, will begin flexing their muscles, so that in time there will be real danger that they would start negotiating with Russia to get the things they want.
I believe that is the greatest danger in connection with this problem of Germany today-the danger that when Germany is reunited or rearmed, because of her interests in the east she will negotiate with her former enemy, Russia. And when that time comes it seems to me there would be little hope that the guarantees indicated by the minister would be sufficiently effective to control the destinies of that country.
It is my view that, rather than a policy of immediate rearmament, the west should proceed step by step in a rearming program. By offering real democracy and better economic conditions to East Germany there would be a basis from which we could reach some solution. As it is, I believe there will be two armed camps standing side by side within a short distance of each other, a condition fraught with many dangers.
There are others with authority and good judgment in these matters who bolster my argument. I would refer first to Dorothy Thompson and Thomas Mann, both of whom believe as I do that German military power would be used eventually for her own interests. Thomas Mann says, as reported in the Citizen of January 20:
The trend of world affairs is menacing, pregnant with disaster.
And then he warns:
Putting yesterday's mortal enemies back in the saddle, the west is scandalizing the peace-loving majority of West Germany.
And so I believe the move to rearm West Germany is a very serious procedure indeed.
I might digress from my argument just to point out what is involved in a third world war. I hold in my hand a copy of the U.S. News and World Report of January 28. On the front page in large red and white letters I find the following: "No need to bomb cities to win wars." I do not agree with the contents of the article to which I want to refer. The article was written by Colonel Richard Leghorn. I do not agree
North Atlantic Treaty
with his arguments because they are fallacious, they are pregnant with disaster for the west. However, I want to indicate what he has to say in regard to the situation now facing the world, should a third world war come upon us. This is what he says:
One hundred assorted modern bombs on target can knock out one half of United States industrial capacity and tens of millions of Americans. The 100 largest cities of the NATO powers in western Europe contain one-quarter of its population and a greater fraction of its industrial capacity. Two hundred bombs on city targets would destroy the western world.
Further on this author indicates that an intercontinental ballistic missile has been invented. This missile can go from continent to continent at a velocity twenty times the speed of sound, and there is no method of defence against it. Therefore, we are facing a serious problem in trying to settle this matter.
My conclusions are not entirely my own. They are also those of our national convention which took place in the early part of last year at Edmonton and the decision of the national council. It, too, is the decision of the world council of churches and many other citizens throughout Canada. There has not come to my desk one letter indicating support of rearming Germany. On the other hand I have received many letters protesting the rearming of Germany at this time.
There are some things that plague the world today which prevent a real solution to the problems of war. The conference table of the United Nations has been plagued with the fact that people who go there with high hopes and sincerity have to work under pretty difficult conditions. I wish to refer to what I think is the basic cause of war today, namely, the international cartelization of the armament industry. Any hope of world peace is bound to be bedevilled as long as that situation exists. It is well known to hon. members that during the first world war Canadian soldiers in France were wounded and shot by machine guns manufactured in Britain. We also know the story of Madame Chiang Kai-shek when the Americans were in China during the last war offering military assistance. The story is told of Madame Chiang Kai-shek coming in with a piece of a Japanese plane of American make shot down over China. We have all these contradictions.
I want to dwell on one important world cartel which in itself proves the point I am trying to make. I refer to international capitalism and those merchants of death. They know no country; they know no patriotism; their allegiance is to one thing and one thing

North Atlantic Treaty
only, namely, the making of profit. They have no compunctions about the deaths they cause; their one idea is centred on the making of profit. I wish to refer to the I. G. Farben company, the great nazi Germany chemical empire.
This great cartel operated during the last war. As a matter of fact it was responsible for the near success of Hitler. In the early days of 1932 when Hitler was coming to power this cartel played an important part in his rise to power. At the Nuremberg trials in 1947 24 leaders of this German dye trust appeared. At that time the conscience of the world was awakened. Perhaps that has all been forgotten since. These 24 leaders appeared before the military tribunal at Nuremberg, and charges were made that the
I.	G. Farben company played an important role in preparing the third reich for aggressive war. This is one of the largest firms in the world. It has 400 participating firms in Germany and over 700 affiliated companies in 104 countries throughout the world where they gained the control. Where they have not direct control, then they control the companies by patents and other policies. The charges laid at these trials were that this company was guilty of wilfully engaging in activities indispensable to Germany's aggressive war.
On November 6, 1932, the Reichstag elections were held. The nazis lost very heavily. There was a conference between Hitler and the leaders of this great cartel. At that time the Farben company was going to cease manufacturing synthetic gasoline; but when they went to Hitler he promised them assistance, and from that time on there was friendship between this important company and Hitler. More than any other thing in the world, this company was responsible for the war machine of Hitler. Indeed the ramifications of this company went so far that they gave money to the Sudeten Germany free corps which was a sabotage association, and it did other work on the frontiers in order to cause trouble.
It is worth noting that Hitler had only a small segment of the people on his side, but he had this huge and powerful industrial concern. When we look through newspaper reports at this time we find that once again this huge chemical firm has been reinstated in all its ramifications all over the world. This company even has its tentacles in Canada. At the Nuremberg trials it was found that seven Canadian companies were in some way connected with this great chemical concern. Until people of good will in the world, people in responsible positions-I am now speaking to this government-are prepared to take
fMr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).!
a stand to decartelize these warmongers, these merchants of death throughout the world who govern and control by their assistance to governments and through their propaganda, we shall not have peace.
As a solution I have a six-point program which I want to put before the government and the house. The policy of the western nations should be: First, to accept the fact that coexistence or no existence is a reality and there can be no victory for either side if a third world war should come. That is the first thing we have to realize and accept.
Second, we must accept the proposition that genuine and permanent check of communist influence is possible only with better ideas, politically, economically and morally, and institute these in world policy at every level.
Third, we must reiterate our faith in the United Nations. I am very happy that the minister of external affairs has expressed this faith in the United Nations in connection with the situation developing in Formosa, and that Canada will again have faith in the United Nations for the solving of the great problems of mankind. We must reiterate our faith in the United Nations as the framework to establish world peace and justice.
Fourth, we must immediately attempt, stage by stage, a reduction in conventional and new weapons.
Fifth, we must set up a world arms control agency under the United Nations to control arms production, both conventional and new weapons.
Sixth, we must set up through the United Nations an agency to break the world-wide cartelization of profit-motivated merchants of death.
We are going to be plagued with this situation. These people have allegiance to international capitalism and to no other ideal. They have no allegiance except to the profit motive. Surely the good will throughout the world, surely governments in responsible positions in the democracies are going to see that something is done about this so that the world will not be faced time and time again with world wars.
In conclusion I want to say that I am against rearming Germany because I do not think that a solution can come through an arms race. The logical thing is to realize that you can never reach the pyramid by which one side will gain over the other enough tactical strength, enough armaments to assure victory.
When speaking at Estevan in 1945 I put forth the proposition that it was a case of finding out how to live with Russia or to die

with her. At that time I expressed the opinion that by the use of technological means at our disposal the western nations, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) said, by going into those areas where there are economic conditions from which communism can grow, and by correcting those difficulties, could gain the opportunity of living in coexistence with the Russians.
We are today fighting an ideological war and we shall not win it by force alone, except the force of conviction that we have the best kind of government in the world, democracy, and by showing that we have moral principles and that we are prepared to establish moral agencies throughout the world.
I think this is the hope and aspiration of all people of good will throughout the world. I only hope that what I have said may have even some small sympathetic reception in the hearts of people who believe, as I do, that war solves no problem.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make my position known in respect to the present resolution, and at the commencement of my remarks may I read what the resolution is:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.
Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose there has been any one decision over the past few years that is so important as the decision which we are called upon to make in this resolution. We have often read in the past of the responsibilities of members of parliament. Sometimes those responsibilities have been depreciated by a cheap sort of journalism. Perhaps it appears that there may be some element of insincerity with our work at times; but when members of parliament come face to face with such a decision as we have to make in voting on this resolution, then those responsibilities are not child's play in any sense. The decision that we are to make in respect to this resolution as far as Canada is concerned may well determine the future course of history.
When facing a responsibility of this kind I cannot help turning my mind back to the time when the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King came into this house, after calling a special session of this parliament, and asked us to vote to declare war on Germany. To me that was perhaps one of the greatest decisions which I have ever had to make in my political life, because at the time my two stepsons and my first-born son were of military age.
North Atlantic Treaty
Of course I followed the events of the war very closely. I am not alone in this. Like the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) and others in this house, I suffered the heartbreaking experience of losing my own son in that war. Such heartbreaking experiences not only tear at one's heart but cause one to think and to think desperately. I followed the events of that war and the events that transpired after the war. I followed with interest the conferences that were held by the big men of the earth, the conferences between President Roosevelt, Prime Minister Churchill, Stalin and later President Truman. I recall the conferences of Yalta and Tehran.
As I followed them closely, wondering how they would affect the future course of history, believe me, I have come to the conclusion that no greater treachery has been perpetrated upon the human race than was accomplished at those conferences. Time and time again we gave a foothold to what is now our enemy and helped it to build its strength to its present powerful position, and which today constitutes a threat to our civilization.
I must admit that as I looked at those things with the emotion that characterizes every human soul I was tempted to adopt an unchangeable decision that I would never, never again vote for any measure that would indicate in the least possible degree the possibility of war, for I determined that never again should I ever have any confidence in those who have the responsibility for determining international policy.
Now we are face to face with another decision, and in facing that great decision I am also faced with the knowledge that I now have another son of military age. But as I think of that other decision and that other son I must also remember that we have another enemy, and an enemy who is perhaps just as ruthless if not more ruthless than the enemy of a few years ago.
We have heard a great deal about German atrocities. I know that we all, each and every one of us, abhor them. Each and every one of us detests them. We do not even like to think of them. It is significant, however, that many speakers in this debate who have mentioned those atrocities have paid little attention to the atrocities of the present enemies of the west. Millions upon millions have been liquidated by Russia and her satellites for no other crime than simply a desire to own their own little farms, and live their own lives freely. We are faced now with that enemy and must now make a decision in respect to it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned I lost one son and I have another who is now

North Atlantic Treaty
of military age, and when I think of them I recall the remarks of an hon. member in this house. I was moved to tears as I heard the concluding remarks of the speech delivered in this house the other day by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). Some of us perhaps think we have suffered, but I would like to refresh our memories by reading a few paragraphs of the hon. member's speech. I quote from page 401 of Hansard of January 20, 1955:
I know, Mr. Speaker, that all my colleagues in the house will bear with me if they find that I have spoken with some emotion an this subject. If I did so, it is perhaps due to the fact that, to a greater extent than anyone else in the house possibly, I have personally been a victim of nazi cruelty. My rather distressed feelings result not only from the fact that I belong to that ethnic group which suffered most, but also because my own uncles, aunts and cousins, consisting of a family of over 60 persons, were tormented and put to death by the nazis. Hon. members I am sure can therefore appreciate that if, notwithstanding the over-all record of nazi cruelty and my own personal grief, I am still led to the conclusion to vote in favour of this resolution, I do so only because, to paraphrase a Shakespearean line:
"Not that I dislike Berlin less,
But because I fear Moscow more".
By your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one more personal remark, and it is this: As I stand here before my colleagues on the floor of this house, and as one of the spokesmen of my ethnic group, I most solemnly declare that I vote for the resolution, but not without a deep ache in my heart caused by my grave doubts, apprehensions and misgivings; and I therefore accompany my vote with a most fervent prayer that, in the wisdom of Him who guides the destiny of us all, this vote may be for the betterment of all mankind.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that the pronoun "Him" is spelled with a capital letter. I suppose those words now written in Hansard will finally be buried in our musty old archives, but though they might be buried there they will not be buried in the eternal record.
I have pointed out that we have another enemy to face. In this regard we have heard a good deal lately about the dangers of German rearmament. I know we are all very conscious of that danger and, as the hon. member for Cartier pointed out, we approach it with some misgiving. We have heard a lot about the German military machine. But the fact of the matter is that we have heard very little from the people who debate in this fashion about the tremendous power and ruthlessness of the enemy who now confronts us, and that enemy is not a German war machine but another war machine more powerful than any the world has ever seen, except perhaps that which is gradually coming into existence through NATO and largely because of the strength of the United States.

I declare that we have no choice, Mr. Speaker. We are faced with an enemy and we face him today. It is not a matter of what might happen in future years following the rearmament of Germany. The important question is what is happening today.
A couple of years ago it was my privilege to visit Germany. I cannot reveal the names of those with whom I spoke, but I will say that on one occasion I had an opportunity of speaking with three or four high German government officials. I believe that experience that evening will perhaps highlight many of the other experiences I have had. Those top ranking German government officials were not nazis. In fact, one gentleman, whose name I am not at liberty to reveal, was on Hitler's liquidation list, managed to escape, and because of his ability and desire to serve his country returned to Germany. He told me that the great desire of those in office in Germany was to bring Germany within the orbit of the free and democratic nations of the world. One might ask what confidence we could have in those words. But if we adopt that attitude we might as well ask what confidence we can have in anyone's word. I felt at the time that there was a great desire on the part of those in top ranking influential positions to bring Germany back-yes, I know, restore her sovereignty- but also back into the place where she would be known as a free nation, and take her place as one of the free nations of the world.
I now want to pass on to another subject that I think is extremely important. It has been mentioned a number of times. I refer to the subject of the necessity for continuing negotiations with the enemy. I say "the enemy". There is no other way to describe them. My hon. friend who has just resumed his seat talked about the possibility of coexistence. I am well aware of what that means. I am not so stupid as to believe that we are not living in a world side by side with the enemy. The propagandists for coexistence mean only one thing. They mean for us to live at peace by granting concessions all along the way to those who are proposing this idea of coexistence. It means negotiation by concession.
The other day the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) argued that progress had been made by negotiation. Let us not ever believe that Moscow has changed or will ever change its ultimate objective. It never will. When we talk about progress by negotiation, we can mean only one thing, namely progress by concession. I have yet to see that we have received any benefit of

negotiation with the Russians. Only the communist imperialists have come out on top. If it is progress at all, it is progress down hill. It must be remembered that you can make progress down hill.
I heard a great deal about this progress by negotiation and about pursuing peaceful means. I know it is a nice phrase. The Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon used it. What I think we must determine is whether or not this enemy of ours is evil. Let us determine that fact first. Is it evil or is it not? If it is evil, then is it right for us to coexist with it and to grant concession to that which is evil? That is the decision we must make. We talk about peaceful means, but what is meant by "peaceful means"? They are nice words; it is a glowing phrase. It is nice to use it, but there is only one thing that phrase "by peaceful means" can mean. "Peaceful means" is a delusion and a snare. It is a delusion and a snare to assume that evil aggression can be overcome by peaceful means.
I do not want to stand here and to sound like one who is anxious to fight or is anxious for war. Over and over again in this debate it has been said that nobody wants war. Nobody hates war any more than do I or other hon. members. But we must face realities with regard to this matter. The only place where peaceful means could be successfully employed is between men of good will; and our communist enemies-I will not call them our communist friends-have proven over and over again that they are not men of good will. Just how far would law enforcement agencies get if they notified the underworld that henceforth every criminal problem would be solved by peaceful means only? If the F.B.I. or the R.C.M.P. and all our police forces were forbidden to use arms and were instructed to resort to peace in opposing criminals and criminal acts, the resulting increase in violence and crime would terrify and demoralize the whole nation. The use of the term "peaceful means" is meaningless when applied to the acts of violence perpetrated by international communism. We must destroy the ability of the communists to inflict injustices upon others or we ourselves must face ultimate destruction. There is no alternative.
As to this particular resolution, may I say this. The masters of the Kremlin are more anxious to weaken and to make ineffective the North Atlantic Treaty Organization than they are to do anything else. They are more interested in pushing the United States out of Europe than in any other political objective today. Why? Because they know
North Atlantic Treaty
that just as long as NATO is effective, they will not be able to move with respect to their political objectives, at least in that part of the world.
Let me now say this, Mr. Speaker. Some of our friends have been warning against the possible dangers in respect of a rearmed Germany, as though when once it is rearmed it is going to turn on us. I suppose that might be a chance we have to take. But let me throw out this thought. If any conflict should break out in Europe, it would not result in a local skirmish; it would result in another world war. We do not want it to come but I say that in that event I would rather have Germany with us than against us.
May I read from an article written by William Henry Chamberlin. Of course there are some people who will perhaps denounce Mr. Chamberlin for his attitude on many things. But in an article he wrote not long ago he throws some light on this picture in respect of the rearming of Germany. I am not going to read it at all, of course, but there is a point here that I think is well worth consideration. He says:
Europe cannot be defended against occupation unless there is at least one strong European power.
I believe the idea of this resolution is to make NATO effective and to make it a strong power. Mr. Chamberlin continues:
Unfortunately not one nation on the continent qualifies under this definition today. It is no exaggeration to say that Germany offers the only hope of playing this role.
This is the particular thought I wanted to bring before you, Mr. Speaker:
. . . the rearming of Germany in alliance with America-
And under this resolution it is an alliance with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
-and the west is the most hopeful means of cracking the iron curtain. The inner rottenness of the Soviet puppet regime in the Soviet zone of Germany was exposed on June 17, 1953, when only the presence of Soviet troops made it possible to put down a widespread spontaneous uprising. Without the backing of Soviet occupation troops the red Quisling regime in the Soviet zone would not last five minutes.
Then the article goes on to say that "the Soviet zone is extremely shaky." The article continues:
Some opponents of German rearming, in and out of Germany, contend that the German people are more interested in national unity than in association with the west. But there is really no such alternative. The Soviet government has never consented to German unification on the only basis that would be acceptable to the overwhelming majority of West Germans, conservatives and socialists alike: free elections accompanied by freedom of speech, press, assembly and political parties. The last "election" in- the Soviet zone late in October followed the usual totalitarian pattern: one

North Atlantic Treaty
official list of candidates, people prodded to the polls by intimidation, a 99-3 per cent majority for the official list.
Skipping a bit in the article, I read this pungent part:
And once the chain of Soviet empire snaps in its weakest link, in the Soviet zone of Germany, the crack-up of the whole jerrybuilt structure of Soviet imperialism in eastern Europe, with repercussions on the dictatorship in Russia, would become a possibility. No wonder Molotov gives the prevention of German rearmament the highest priority in his foreign policy aims.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, it is an obvious thing of late that the prevention of German rearmament has had top priority in the Moscow propaganda program that permeates the world. I do not want to say that men have not spoken in this debate with a good deal of conviction, but I say that that conviction must be very naive if they cannot see that. Many speakers have expressed their approval of the high level of debate, and I do not want to minimize it. Should any members take a position that is opposite to mine, I am not going to call them communists. I am not very much concerned with whether or not a man carries a communist card. I am concerned about the men who follow the communist line. I say that it is the most illogical thing for one to bellow: "I hate communism, I do not like communism, communism is a thing I abhor", and then turn around and do the very things that the communists want them to do. That is illogical, and I cannot see how a person can be so naive that he cannot see that.
As far as I can visualize the world scene, I cannot see that there is any other position to take, with all our misgivings, than to vote for the resolution. We have Germany, a country with a high degree of national unity, with proved industrial and military capacity, with a negligible communist fifth column, and a bitter sense of grievance against the Soviet union. What more could we ask in the way of a co-partner with us in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization? It is true that Germany has been our enemy in the last two world wars, but it is not a new thing for a former enemy to become an ally any more than it is a new thing, as has happened today, for a former ally to become our enemy. It is not a new thing.
One can talk about Germany, the ruthlessness of Germany and so forth, but I think we are all aware that we cannot tag the German people with that. The speech made by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) yesterday is most revealing. The German people came under the dynamic leadership of a dictator but there were circumstances involved in those years and, if I may say so, they fell for it. That does not

mean to say that the nature of these people is ruthless. Many of us have German communities in our constituencies. We mingle with these people and they are just as good citizens and good people as any of us. Personally I should like to keep them as my friends.
It is better to have this powerful nation as our friend in the face of any threatened war than to have her on the side of our enemy. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I take my position with our leader and other members of this group in supporting the resolution.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even before this debate was initiated, I had decided to support the protocol of accession of the Federal Republic of Germany to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I have not changed my mind. However, after considering some of the speeches delivered on the subject, I have thought it advisable to state my reasons for taking this stand.
In spite of all the propaganda to which we have been subjected for several months, when attempts were made to demonstrate to us the importance of the part Germany might be called upon to play in the defence of peace, I do not hesitate to give the benefit of the doubt to our allies of the NATO organization, and to grant that they are sincere in their efforts to achieve their aims.
On the other hand, we must not overlook the fact that in the countries where the problem has been referred to parliament, and even here in Canada, considerable opposition has developed.
Are the members of this last group equally sincere in claiming that Germany's entry into NATO would render peace more uncertain still and even make for added friction? I would feel like answering in the affirmative, which is the same as saying-and that is my sincere feeling in the matter-that it is possible to be opposed to the protocol and yet be no communist.
Between these two alternatives we must objectively seek the truth. It is impossible for a citizen of France not to remember or to feel in his very flesh the sufferings and misfortune which have thrice fallen upon his country in a 70-year period. For a German citizen it is not easy to forget either that these same misfortunes and sufferings, for which he is himself responsible, have by no means improved his lot even though, once out of three times, he emerged victorious from this venture.

And the memory of these sad events in both these countries is sufficient to cause an important section of the population to hesitate and to wonder whether armaments are really the best way of maintaining peace.
Under these conditions, the reasons expressed from all sides may quite properly be justifiable, by those who oppose the motion as well as by those who support it.
I should be quite inclined to believe that, in both of these opposing groups, there exists an equally sincere loyalty to the country and an unequivocal will to protect her from communism. To my mind, the difference lies in the appraisal of the means to be adopted.
In our case, however, the problem must be set in an altogether different manner. It should be discussed-publicly I mean-more calmly and more objectively. I exclude from this remark, of course, most of the speeches made in this house, and particularly the brilliant report made by the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
There is being created among the public in the United States as well as in Canada some sort of mass hysteria, some kind of mass psychosis of which the leaders themselves in the end are not entirely free.
But, and this is true of masses as well as of individuals, the moves that are made in such a condition of nervous tension are often unreasoned, and they are sometimes detrimental and fraught with unfavourable consequences.
I readily admit that those who support the cold war are largely responsible for that condition of tension in which we live; but the cold war is not always fought on only one side of the barricade; and even among those who are beyond all question on the side of right and justice-I mean our allies in NATO -there is some overdoing which tends to foster that nervous condition so incompatible with calm judgment and cool reasoning.
After all, we should know chalk from cheese. A good example of the errors which are accepted offhand by whole populations who, owing to well-timed propaganda, seem unable to think for themselves and to react, is precisely that mutual defence treaty agreed to by the United States and nationalist China. We have proof of it at this very time when we can put our fingers, so to speak, on the very serious complications that are threaten-50433-33
North Atlantic Treaty
ing us as the allies of the United States, a consequence of that treaty which seems to me unjustifiable and indefensible.
Another instance of such exaggeration, which this time is shown by the Canadian government and but too easily accepted by a benumbed population-so to speak-as a result of well-organized propaganda, is our overexpenditure of public moneys for our participation in the Korean war and the sending and maintaining in Europe of the troops we are keeping there now, for our own protection perhaps, but mainly to protect countries which hesitate to a considerable degree to contribute to their own protection.
I express the hope that if parliament ratifies the entry of Germany into NATO-I hope and wish it will be so-measures will be taken to bring back as soon as possible to Canada the men and the materiel which we have in Europe at the present time.
By thus facing realities, we will ease the heavy burden of the Canadian taxpayers and keep our contribution to the defence of the west within reasonable limits.
In that respect, may I be permitted to quote a short extract from the editorial which Le Soleil published on January 22, 1955, under the following title:
Ottawa considers the German problem.
The writer devotes a few lines to the problem in general, then states precisely what I have said, that certain European countries seem to drag their feet, so to speak, with respect to the setting-up of their own defence. The editorialist then adds:
Such being the case, ratification by the Canadian parliament will in fact have but very little effect on German rearmament.. We should be humble enough to admit it. In this way we would be able to equate our international commitments with our small population. In this connection Canada could think of repatriating at least the ground troops we maintain in Germany, at colossal expense, quite out of proportion with their military usefulness, in return for our agreeing to the rearmament of a nation which, through its own fault or that of world politicians, has twice drawn Canada into war in the space of a single generation.
Nevertheless, even though we must be careful, even though we must guard against propaganda and try to look at things objectively when everything conspires to rush us, we must recognize that we are, at this time, faced with a dilemma which must be solved.
Shall we allow the German republic to rearm and to enter that group of countries with which we are associated for our collective

North Atlantic Treaty
defence on an equal footing or shall we allow her to rot in a state of forced neutrality, inaction and repression, which may be without danger when it is chosen out of free will, but which readily becomes a cause of the most serious disorder when imposed by coercion from outside?
In my humble opinion, it is not so much a question of deciding whether Germany will be rearmed or not, but whether or not she will recover her freedom. In spite of all the ills she has in fact brought upon Europe and the whole of humanity, by reason of her unjustified aggressions, it appears to me that we have no right and that it is not wise to keep this vanquished people indefinitely captive. That would be, moreover, a means of redeeming the errors committed after the last two wars when we seemed to be wanting to tighten to the limit the grip intended to crush an overly venturesome enemy. Undoubtedly, the rearming of Germany carries probable risks, but I sincerely believe that these risks are smaller than the ones we are running by letting this country fume under inaction and repression.
History does not relate a single instance where a young, strong and vigorous nation might have been kept for a long time in trusteeship, as has been the case, since the end of the last war, of both Germany and Japan. That might be possible with decaying and decadent nations, but it will never be possible in the case of present-day Germany.
We must also never lose sight of the fact that an opponent as treacherous and as unscrupulous as communist Russia will never be completely thwarted by armed might only. Even in defeat, they will continue to instil into our veins the poison of their doctrine.
Besides adequate military preparedness, in which I am willing to include German rearmament, we must put into play such other forces, moral forces, as honesty of intentions, superiority and integrity of purpose, honesty of means, a sincere desire for Christian justice, not only for ourselves and our allies, but also for our opponents and for the vanquished. Those are many factors of great importance in our struggle against the communists; factors which are not to be found, I do not hesitate to say, on their side, but that we must make sure to find here, in the heart and soul of free peoples.
I shall vote for the motion to approve the protocol, not so much because it allows Germany to rearm, but rather because it makes

her free again, hoping indeed that, in her love for liberty, she may join us in our efforts to repel communism.
