speechtext:
North Atlantic Treaty
However, we must do our duty. I am confident that we will give no respite to our common enemy, that we will take all necessary steps to fight that enemy and that we will agree to make more sacrifices to check the march of enemy forces.
German rearmament and the entry of Germany into NATO is a preventive measure which will make Russia think.
I am sure everyone wishes to see the present international disagreements which cause so much grief come to an end and hopes that mutual understanding may give us long years of peace.
However, we must always be ready for anything that may happen; in troubled times like these, the motto si vis pacem, para helium is justified. We are threatened by the forces of evil, well provided with munitions of war; we must therefore arm ourselves accordingly in order to repel the inhuman hordes that are preparing to swoop down upon the world.
I cannot conclude my remarks without challenging some statements made by two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne). Those two members miss no opportunity of expressing their antagonism towards the government.
The member for Three Rivers deplores the fact that our country is always trying to play a leading part in international ventures. If he will only refer to Hansard, he will see that at the very moment when our war effort seemed to me far above our strength, his own leader thought that we were not doing enough. I am sure that the hon. member for Three Rivers would then take the first opportunity to change his mind as to the part our country is called upon to play in international disputes or international relations between Canada and other nations. I admit that, in certain circumstances, our efforts went beyond what could be expected of us. But where the hon. member becomes utterly ridiculous is when he inquires why the minister (Mr. Pearson) attended the meeting held in London by those we call the "big powers", especially, he adds, without having been invited.
The hon. member admits that we have interests to protect in Europe but he fails to see why we should seek information on the subject which was under examination at that conference: the rearming of Germany.

For my part I think that it was necessary for our Secretary of State for External Affairs to remain in touch with the question, in such a way as to make it possible for him to give facts and reasons to his colleagues in this Canadian parliament.
I would like to take this opportunity- though I would not like to be accused of flattery-to express to the Secretary of State for External Affairs my very sincere personal admiration for the leading part he has played in the United Nations and abroad. He has caused our country to be better known and, in so doing, he has informed all nations concerned of our firm determination to defend peace. At the same time, he has most certainly contributed to the solution of economic questions and of various other problems, to the benefit of this country of ours.
German rearmament is of very weighty consequence for humanity as a whole and everything done to promote it will be such as to serve our cause.
Our minister may have no lesson to take from me, but he will nevertheless be well-advised to remain in constant touch with all questions which are of close or remote interest to us and, on occasion, to make his views known. So far his presence has been of service to our own country and to our cause.
As regards the member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne), he also is bent on criticizing the government. In his opinion, parliament should have been convened sooner. Did that dear colleague of ours want us to make a decision before the very countries which, according to the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), are primarily interested in studying the matter, had made their decision known as to the advisability of admitting Western Germany into NATO and consequently of granting this new ally the right to rearm? I say to these two members to agree with one another. One of them claims that we are proceeding ahead of time and the other, who shares the same political views, states that we are not proceeding quickly enough and that we should decide matters even before the parties primarily interested have made a decision. This I say with the best possible good will and spirit. Besides, it is not the first time that opinions do not seem to converge on the same point in the ranks of the opposition in this house.
However, such partisan criticism will not prevent, I am sure, a majority of members on the opposition benches as well as on the government benches from voting for the motion now before this house.

Our stand, which is not, I repeat, an aggressive one, will permit us to look to the future with greater serenity. God grant that the action we are now taking will bring us that peace we all pray for, and that the future of every country will be such that we will be glad to live there in human conditions which can materialize only through the behaviour of those who have but one wish: that the world may have peace and unity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been stressed by many who have already spoken in this debate that at this time we face a difficult problem and an even more difficult decision. I agree with that. Perhaps I might go even a little further and say it is not only a difficult but an agonizing decision that will have to be made in this house within a matter of hours.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the previous speakers. I have listened with a great deal of respect to nearly all the previous speakers. But I regret that a small minority has seen fit to lower, in my estimation, the high plane on which this debate has been conducted by making inferences and casting aspersions on those who may be voting in opposition to this motion.
We differ in this house individually and along party lines. We comprise five groups, Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F., Social Credit, and independents. We differ in outlook, viewpoint and program. But I have always taken pride in the belief that we do not differ in our love of this country, in our patriotism, and in our anti-communism and anti-communist line. We are all the same on that. Therefore I think I am quite in order in saying I regret that for reasons known only to themselves a few hon. members of this house have cast aspersions, such as fellow travellers, followers of the commie line, and commie stooges, upon those who do not agree with them.
I listened with a great deal of interest to all that has been said thus far, and particularly to the speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I could not but help note the great similarity in the proposals and terminology to that which was used over 30 years ago. In the past few days we have heard a great deal about the threat of Russian might; about the fact that we need a bulwark in Germany and that the price of Germany's admission to NATO will be the partial rearmament of that country.
North Atlantic Treaty
That expression rang a bell, so I went down to the library and found my memory had served me well. The request for our support of this motion at this time is similar to the request made for the same purpose over 30 years ago, not at that time by the western powers or the United Nations, but by the German foreign office. Gustav Stresemann was chancellor and minister of foreign affairs in Germany from 1923 to 1929, and I would like to quote a statement by that gentleman in order to demonstrate the similarity to the present proposal. I quote from "Stresemann and the Revision of Versailles", page 139:
It was the danger of a bolshevik penetration of Germany's eastern provinces, and the accompanying danger of insurrection, which caused Stresemann to demand an easing of the disarmament restrictions. Referring to allied protests against the citizens' militia which had sprung into existence everywhere in Germany, he addressed this warning to the west:
"If the path is cleared for a victorious advance of bolshevism by (allied insistence upon complete disarmament of Germany), then bolshevism will not halt at the Rhine, not at the channel, unless it is stopped in Germany."
That was not from the speech of a few days ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; those words were spoken just after the first world war.
There were other items, factual, interesting, and logical, which drew my attention but one other statement also rang a bell. That was the important statement wherein the minister stressed that the rearmament of Germany as a member of the NATO family would be governed by controls and restrictions, and completely supervised. We all welcomed that statement and appreciated the detail into which the minister went in dealing with it. But it is exactly what was heard 32 years ago.
Article 8 of the covenant of the league of nations is of great relevance in this regard. Perhaps hon. members would like to read it when time permits. But on that point I would like to quote from what I understand is a very authoritative book, namely "The Encyclopaedia of the Social Sciences". I quote from page 480 of volume IX:
The treaty of Versailles imposed drastic disarmament upon the defeated powers; it also declared (art. 8) "that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest point consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations" and entrusted to the council of the league of nations the task of drawing up plans of reduction, which should be subject to reconsideration at least every 10 years. Members of the league also undertook to interchange full and frank information as to the scale of their armaments and military programs.
The ideas advanced at that time under the sponsorship of the western powers within the league of nations were similar to the

North Atlantic Treaty
arguments being advanced today in support of the protocol now before this house. Yet despite the controls and agreements drawn up after the first world war under the organization of the democratic powers, we landed into a second world war.
I admit, and believe, it is the sincere hope and belief of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that this time it will be different; that this time rearmament and control under the auspices of the western powers will not lead to another world war. I earnestly hope the minister is correct. But history repeats itself; and the arguments advanced so far do not, in my opinion, contain enough convincing evidence to show me that they are not out of the realm of prophecy and the problematical. There has not yet been given a sufficient cogency of argument to show that, just as we did not know of a Hitler at the end of the last world war, we may not in the future see in Germany the rise of somebody else, be he a dictator of nazism or a dictator of communism, both to be abhorred. Those two points, Mr. Speaker, I bring in only by the way, but they are important.
I noticed that almost without exception those who have spoken said they had arrived at the conclusion that this matter could not be discussed from a viewpoint of emotionalism but that it could be considered only from a standpoint of realism. I cannot understand that kind of thinking. In fact I completely disagree with it. I make no apologies whatsoever for the fact that, in the time I have left, I intend to speak on an emotional basis because real emotionalism is based upon deep understanding and deep feeling, and deep feeling is engendered by a study and analysis of the facts.
Because we face a most difficult and agonizing decision that must be made on the floor of the House of Commons, to the best of my ability, for a great many days, I have been trying to study and to analyse the facts. I have under my desk at the present moment something in the neighbourhood of 20 authoritative books and publications issued by the government, and which are to be found in the library. It is on the basis of study and analysis of these facts that I have a deep feeling, and therefore speak with deep emotion.
What are the facts? They are as follows. It is only ten years, approximately, since the end of the second world war. What was the purpose of that world war which ended only about ten years ago? The purpose was to disarm Germany. What again is the fact? Ten years later we are being asked in this House of Commons to cast our votes in favour of a partial rearmament of the country that we fought to disarm. Canada is a nation 
large in area and in influence but small in population. In our lifetime Canada has gone to war twice. What for? To disarm Germany.
In discussing this matter, Mr. Speaker, should we forget the price Canada paid? I do not think we should. In 1914 the population of Canada was 7,879,000. We played our part in going to war to stop aggression and disarm Germany. What price did Canada pay? The price was 56,634 dead and 149,732 wounded. In 1939 Canada had a population of 11,315,000, and again we went to war. For what purpose? To disarm Germany. What price did Canada pay in that war? The price she paid was 41,992 dead and 53,145 wounded.
That was the price in life and limb. In two wars to disarm Germany, what was the Canadian price in goods or in money, if you want to put it that way? According to the government records, it cost Canada $2 billion to wage the first world war and $20-25 billion to wage the second world war. We are obligated to take care of the dependents of our dead, and our wounded and their dependents. According to the department I contacted here a few days ago-and I want to thank them for their co-operation-as a result of those two world wars, in allowances to the dependents of the dead and the wounded until December 31 of last year-some 26 days ago- it had cost Canada $1,994,947,807. But that is not the end. The Department of National Defence has required money, to a great extent because of German aggression and the threat of German aggression and in later years, of course, because of another threat; but it is all because of war. Mr. Speaker, if we take all those publications called "Canada's Defence Program" issued by the Department of National Defence and add the figures together, we find that from 1919 up to and including the estimates for this fiscal year-excluding the cost of waging war, and excluding pensions-our defence expenditures have reached the fantastic sum of $19,828 million.
Let us for a moment just recapitulate the price Canada has paid, mostly to disarm Germany in two world wars. Here is the way it goes. In two wars, 98,626 dead and 202,877 wounded. That is the cost in life and limb. Then there is the cost of waging two world wars, namely $22J billion. Add to that the cost of pensions, and you get $24i billion. Then if you add the cost of the defence department, you get $44,047,947,807.
It is only ten years since the war to disarm Germany ended. We are asked to forgive and forget. Sometimes it is a good thing to do so. We are asked to believe that there has been a change in the national viewpoint and outlook in that important country. We are asked to believe that under control that country can be directed. We are asked to forget the price

Canada paid. We are asked to forget that, up until ten years ago, Germany was the nation that prosecuted, persecuted, imprisoned, tortured, crucified and murdered millions of innocents. We are asked to believe that all that has changed.
Mr. Speaker, it is my own personal and humble opinion that Canada could do more for peace and the guarantee of peace if we would expend our every effort and any monej we can spare to teach the new generation of Germans the meaning and practice of liberty, freedom and democracy rather than to rearm the generation that negated those principles throughout their entire lifetime.
I know there are many arguments in favour of supporting the resolution. I have heard it said that irrespective of what we do in the House of Commons this is a fait accompli and we cannot do anything about it. I agree that is correct. I have heard it said that even if it were not a fait accompli we cannot and should not try to keep Germany a secondary world power and keep her out of the family of nations. I can agree with that statement too. I have heard it said that even if this were not a fait accompli Germany will eventually become a sovereign nation, that she will rearm partially or fully and there is nothing we can do about it. I am inclined to agree with that, too.
But, sir, in view of the fact that it is only ten years since the last war, viewing the past record of Germany, viewing history and what it teaches, I say there is one thing that we can do, at least there is one thing I can do as a Canadian citizen honoured to have a voice and a vote on the floor of the House of Commons. I can decline to put my stamp of approval on the rearmament of Germany at the present time, and that is the way J intend to vote. Emotionalism? Perhaps. But it is based on deep feeling, and the deep feeling is based upon facts.
Two generations of Canadians have gone down under German guns, and at this time, with all the evidence that is before us, I cannot see myself giving approval to what might mean a third generation of Canadians having to face German guns.
As I said when I started, Mr. Speaker, it is a difficult matter requiring a difficult decision, a decision that is agonizing for all of us. I appreciate all the arguments that have been put forward in favour of the motion. I appreciate the arguments that have been put forward by those who oppose it. I hold all those who are going to vote for the motion in the deepest respect. I pay particular honour to my own leader who, because of conscience, conviction and judgment, has come to a different decision from some of the rest of us.
North Atlantic Treaty
So, Mr. Speaker, because I feel this way, because my feelings are based on facts, I intend when the time comes to stand in my place and be counted in opposition to the rearming of Germany at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be comparatively brief. I am one of those who feel that diplomacy with Russia is carried on better today with a sword in one hand and a treaty in the other than with a treaty alone. That is a harsh thing to have to say on Robert Burns' day, who sang of the time when men shall brothers be for a' that, but I think we have to realize the facts that face us in the world and not engage in wishful thinking when we are debating an issue such as the one now before us.
Two weeks ago deputations came here to call on us. A group of these men and women tramped out in the snow in front of the building a message which read, "Don't rearm the nazis". It was interesting to note that the message could be seen only from one particular point in the building, and only when the sun cast a shadow at a particular time of the day. At other times and from other positions the message, "Don't rearm the nazis" faded until it was unintelligible, until it became nothing more than depressions in the snow. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that much of what we have heard in support of that message, "Don't rearm the nazis", has had its origin in a comparatively narrow point of view, and that when we stand back and view all the aspects of the situation we must come to realize that at this time there is probably no other course open to us.
I think we come to that conclusion because "Don't rearm the nazis" is a negative attitude. On the other hand the entry of Germany into NATO, bringing her once again into the family of nations, is a positive step toward world understanding and world peace. In this connection I should like to pay particular tribute to one ethnic group in Canada and the attitude they have taken on this question. I have made a particular effort to discuss this matter with a number of leaders of the Jewish community, and I have invariably found, just as has been expressed in the house by two members who are of that particular ethnic group, that they approach this resolution and what it entails with misgivings, with unhappiness, but they are prepared to accept it because they feel it is in the best interests of all of us. I think that is a mark of true Canadianism.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that one of the responsibilities of the house, if not the major responsibility, is to lead Canada and

North Atlantic Treaty
its people, and to make our own decisions once all aspects of a situation have been studied and we have heard all sides of an argument. In this respect-and it is regrettable-I think in the past few months the government have defaulted because they have made no effort to inform the people of Canada, as they should have informed them, of all aspects of this question. The government point of view may be well known in Bonn, Germany, Paris, London and all the other places to which these perambulating ministers go, but lamentably the facts are not and have not been well known to the people of Canada. I think perhaps the Gallup poll taken a little while ago which indicated that almost three-quarters of the people of Canada could not name one single cabinet minister is an indication of the lack of effort on the part of these hon. gentlemen to get their story across to the people of Canada.
One more point, Mr. Speaker. In February, 1954, speaking in Bonn, Germany, at a dinner for Dr. Adenauer, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said:
It may be, however, that European unity in itself cannot be expected to furnish an answer to the problems that face western Europe. Perhaps the time has now come to consider whether some of the steps towards closer integration, which we must take if our concept of civilization is not to perish, should be taken within the larger framework of the North Atlantic community. It would be difficult for me at this stage to particularize. But I suggest that we should perhaps be seeking solutions to the problems continuing to face you of achieving greater unity in Europe in a wider context and possibly in pursuit of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty. It has become increasingly clear, I think, to all members of the NATO and to those many countries who are associated with us throughout the free world that our very survival and our continued development in freedom and in peace depends upon our ability to look beyond national barriers and to make them somewhat less artificial and more satisfactory.
There was more in the same vein. That was a year ago, and I think it is regrettable that in the year that has passed this government has not taken more forward-looking steps and more concrete action to implement the suggestions made by the Prime Minister at that time. There is no particular use going around the world preaching this sort of thing unless we are in a position to follow it up and do what we can to bring it about. Honeyed words without action to back them up are of as little value in international affairs as they have been here in Canada. To bring Germany into NATO and let NATO remain static is not going to be a lasting solution to the problems about which we have heard so much in the last few days.
I think the government would be well advised to go back and examine these suggestions of the Prime Minister, this promise

inferentially held out of something that will be done by NATO under article 2, to see just what they are going to do to implement the proposition set forth a year ago.
I shall vote for this motion and for ratification of the treaties, not on any emotional basis, not because of any reason other than that, having examined the facts of the case and having listened to the presentations made in the house, it is my firm conviction that a vote for this motion is a vote for peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been said on various occasions during this debate, the decision we have to take following the motion made by the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is of the highest moment.
For a great number of Canadians, the painful memory of the last years following the second world war is not without a morrow, and the rearmament of Western Germany brings to mind a page of history that is not easily forgotten. We remember with much grief the considerable loss of lives our nation has suffered at the hands of Hitler's men, and the wounds inflicted upon our people in concentration camps are not yet entirely healed.
But from the clear, brilliant and complete comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I gather that the decision we will reach should borrow from reason and realistic judgment that which the heart refuses to understand.
We can more easily understand the approval of this motion, when we recall the confusion caused among the free nations by France's refusal to accept the plan for a European defence community.
At that moment we feared that all the efforts made to maintain unity among western democracies would be of no avail and that a gap exceedingly hard to close had rent the wall of collective security which we had endeavoured to build against communist imperialism. Luckily for us, repeated efforts have made possible a new plan which we are called upon to ratify today and whose aim is approximately that of the European defence community.
Like many others, I received representations to the effect that the rearming of Western Germany could one day work against us.
It is certain that any international agreement is not riskproof. However, a study of the results which will follow the ratification of the protocol is enough to dispel any doubts

and make one decide in favour of the motion. Moreover, the clauses which limit the rearming of Western Germany and which are incorporated into the agreement remove a good deal of the fears that have been expressed.
Perhaps we might have better reason to fear the rearmament of Eastern Germany, which is already an accomplished fact, for who, among the free nations of the world, will dare say that in that part of Germany now under Russian occupation, they need more than one hundred thousand constables, abundantly equipped with tanks and artillery, to maintain peace and order. We all recognize that such a force under Russian control is nothing but a link in the powerful organization set up by Russia in order to make its ascendancy over the world more easily felt.
This decision to rearm our former enemy, which the latter is accepting without compulsion, not only is a direct result of the principles embodied in NATO, but also finds a justification in the continuous opposition raised by the Russians and the relentless stubbornness they show each time the question of an agreement on the unification of Germany comes up.
Moreover, this rearmament is always associated with the principle stated in the Potsdam agreement, namely, to unify Germany for the security of all nations.
Surely, this rearming of western Germany is a sad necessity, but it is the imperative duty of free nations to maintain all the forces required to prevent and deter aggression.
The experience of the last few years and recent events clearly show that the countries behind the iron curtain will be ready to stop their imperialistic march only when they realize that the wall of collective security that we are building in conjunction with our allies is unconquerable. This measure is another stone in the masonry of this wall and it would be unfortunate if Canada, by rejecting it, were to be an obstacle to the laying of this stone.
The welfare of nations in the face of communism requires a security based on the solidarity of all democratic countries. Once this security has been achieved, we all hope that it will then be possible to turn our efforts and our energy to the improvement of the common good in the peace we have been seeking for so long and which we pray divine Providence to grant us.

I believe that parliament more and more should undertake responsibility in making decisions of this kind. I am rather disappointed that we are in the nature of a consultative body, asked to place the stamp of approval on decisions that have been made on our behalf by the minister. I realize that this is necessary in the diplomatic world today, but I do feel that on matters of general policy such as this it should be possible for the government to seek the feeling of the house. Along with other hon. members I think this house could well have met last fall to give more serious consideration to the matter now before us.
We find many hon. members rising and expressing deep concern and grave doubts regarding the wisdom of the step we are now taking. It is only logical that there are going to be differences in conclusions. I think it inconceivable that when so many hon. members are undecided, finding it difficult, as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) did last night, to reach a decision on this matter, there should not be differences in conclusions. I think that is a test of the strength of a democratic government. Only under an authoritarian or totalitarian regime do you find conformity with government policy a necessary thing.
I find it a little difficult to understand the attitude revealed by one or two members who have spoken, who seem to indicate that once the government has laid down its position on a particular matter, then it becomes automatically in the best interests of the country and those who oppose and who hold contrary views are acting against the best interests of the country. We had one speech along those lines last evening, in which an hon. member expressed surprise that there should be some members who have the temerity to question the wisdom of what the government is proposing to do. I believe that, certainly in the field of international affairs as with domestic affairs, a difference of opinion is to be desired. Just because there is uniformity of opinion does not mean that when a mistake is made the consequences of that mistake are any less serious. I think the

North Atlantic Treaty
Globe and Mail Struck that note in an editorial, when it pointed out that while the C.C.F. might be mistaken, at least they were bringing to the attention of the house many of the serious doubts that had existed in the minds of the people of Canada. That is our job as an opposition, and I for one have no apology whatsoever to make for taking issue with the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The high level of the debate, with few exceptions which are hardly worthy of note, indicates that we can look forward in the future to a discussion of international affairs on a sane and sober level. In the way it is handling this problem the house can set an example to the country as a whole so that Canadian citizens will not find themselves in the position of those who were described by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) the other night when, at page 382 of Hansard, he said:
I believe that a good many serious-minded, loyal citizens of this country have possibly been silenced for fear that they might be classed as communists or communist sympathizers.
That such a situation could exist in Canada is a matter of serious regret, because it offers a threat to our time-honoured tradition of free speech and discussion. Those who resort to the tactics which might have brought about this situation have nothing to be proud of, because they are weakening the very fabric of our democratic system.
Many speakers have referred to the fact that the labour progressive party were quite active in trying to influence members of parliament in the past month or so; but to use this as an excuse for voting for the motion is absurd and ridiculous, to say the least. If an hon. member is going to allow himself to be influenced one way or the other, directly or indirectly, by what the communist party says, then I suggest he is placing in the hands of this discredited fragment of our population an influence and power far out of proportion to their position in the political life of this country. I am quite certain that hon. members are capable of deciding on issues of this kind without being influenced, as I say, one way or the other by the group I have just mentioned. It is rather regrettable that one or two hon. members have sought, strictly for political purposes, to create the impression that anyone who is voting against the motion therefore must have been influenced into that position by this campaign.
I am not going to be told by the labour progressive party how to vote, directly or indirectly, one way or the other. I have no respect for that organization. They opposed

me in the last election, and throughout my political experience I have had a great deal of trouble with them. For hon. members to seek cover on this particular issue by pointing to this delegation and using that as an excuse for going along with the rearming of Germany is to take a very weak position indeed.
In his address to the house last Thursday the Secretary of State for External Affairs put forth certain reasons why he felt the house should support the motion. Among other things he suggested that the rearming of West Germany would serve to unite the western democracies and knit closer together the members of the North Atlantic community. With this point of view I cannot agree. In my judgment no single issue in recent years has done more to divide the nations of the western world than this very question that is before the house today.
Other hon. members have pointed out that a motion similar to this was passed in the British House of Commons only by virtue of the fact that there were wholesale abstentions in the house vote. As the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) pointed out, there were around 100 Conservative members of the British House of Commons who did not go along with the government on this particular vote. I will grant you that some of the members may not have voted for other reasons, but in this instance it indicates an unusually large number of members, normally supporting the government, not going along with the Churchill government on this issue.
We know that a minority of the members of the British House of Commons voted on this matter. We know that when the matter was first brought before the national assembly in France the move to support German rearmament was defeated. The matter was introduced a week or so later; and after Mendes-France, with his tremendous prestige, had made it a vote of confidence and had wrapped up a package deal which included a social security measure, he was able to get it through the French assembly. But it must be pointed out that on that occasion the majority of the French assembly did not vote for it. I think the figures show that only 281 out of 627 deputies voted to rearm West Germany. Therefore it is correct to say that the majority of the members of the national assembly in France did not apnrove of German rearmament.
Opposition in France to German rearmament is not restricted to the communist party. As a matter of fact perhaps the most vociferous of the opponents of German rearmament have been the de Gaullists, the extreme

right wingers, and of course the M.R.P., the Roman Catholic party in France. So those who would suggest that objection to German rearmament is confined to the communists should pause and reflect, because if they follow that line of argument to its logical conclusion they are condemning most of the people in the western democracies as fellow travellers or dupes of the communists. I suggest that when we consider this problem we should dismiss from our minds any thought that decisions, apart from decisions made by the communists themselves, are made on any other basis than that of sober consideration of the problems involved.
But while France and Great Britain accepted the rearmament of West Germany very reluctantly and with very grave misgivings, the opposition to German rearmament is more solid in West Germany itself. To judge from the remarks made by some members in this debate one might almost get the impression that the German people are on bended knee crying out to us for justice and demanding that we give them arms. We are told that we cannot deny the German people their place in the family of nations, that we cannot deny the West Germans the right to rearm; and when those arguments are put forth one gets the distinct impression that the German people are crying out for this right. My intelligence would indicate that the reverse seems to be the case, and I would suggest that if this proposed rearmament of West Germany is to go through in its final stages it will depend largely on our ability to sell that idea to the German people themselves.
Perhaps the greatest obstacle to the rearmament of West Germany will be opposition in that part of Germany itself. The people of Germany have been the victims of German militarism in the past, and they are not anxious to saddle themselves once again with the military cliques which in the past have proved so disastrous to the continuance of German democratic institutions. It would appear that in so far as the people of West Germany are concerned, rearmament will have to be brought about as the result of outside pressure.
It seems ironical that just a few short years ago we were saying we were so worried about German militarism, and now we are setting out to convince the German people that they ought to rearm, that they ought once more to set out on the path which has had such tragic consequences not only for the people of Germany themselves but for the peoples of the world.
I agree with the statement made last Thursday by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who said: "Does it not seem tragic and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I had been discussing the remarkable recovery of West Germany from the effects of world war II, and had suggested that this was largely due to the fact that an unarmed West Germany has been able to devote her energies to peaceful pursuits. That perhaps is one of the reasons the German people are reluctant at this time to take on the burden of armaments.
I suggest that if we give the Germans time to build and time to purge themselves of the effects of 12 years of nazi brutality, West Germany could become a tower of strength in the democratic world. It is not an easy task to counteract the long period of nazi indoctrination of German youth. The Germans must have time to complete this task and to build enduring democratic institutions. Nothing can make that task more difficult, or perhaps wellnigh impossible, than the restoration to

North Atlantic Treaty positions of power in Germany of a German military caste. Whatever may be the reasons advanced in support of West German rearmament at this time, let us not pretend too much concern over the German right to rearm, a right which at the present time they do not wish to exercise.
The point of view which I think best expresses German opinion is that enunciated by Erich Ollenhauer, leader of the German social democratic party. According to a report in the London Observer of September 26, 1954, Mr. Ollenhauer summed up his position quite tersely in these words:
First, no West German rearmament before another attempt at agreement with Russia about German reunification and on all-European security. Second, even in the event of failure of such a happening, no irrevocable integration of Western Germany into a supranational western system, and third, German conciliation with France even at the price of postponed German rearmament.
I suggest that the fulfilment of the conditions laid down by this West German statesman would do more to contribute to the building of western unity than the present efforts to force West German rearmament both on Germany herself and on a reluctant and suspicious western Europe.
I referred a moment ago to the proposition that German reunification should be a prior goal to any talk of rearmament. Among Germans in both east and west reunification is and will be a burning issue. One thing is certain; there can be no possibility of a settled and peaceful Europe as long as Germany is artificially divided into east and west. West German rearmament must be considered in the light of this fact. The question that naturally arises on this point is this. Will West German rearmament now help or hinder efforts toward peaceful reunification? On the strength of the evidence at hand I believe that the rearmament of West Germany at this time will make reunification more difficult than ever.
When we have an armed West Germany the logical consequence will be that we will have yielded whatever bargaining power we now possess. The Russians will hold the trump card, for they alone will be in a position to bargain with West Germany on the question of reunification. Russia alone could satisfy the German desire for a united Germany. And since, generally speaking, nations are motivated by self-interest, what reason have we to believe that an armed sovereign West Germany would not at some time in the future make a deal with the Russians?
The minister referred to a quotation the other day which went something like this: "Those who will not learn from the lessons of

history are doomed to repeat it." When the minister made that statement my mind went back to 1939 and the German-Russian nonaggression pact of that period. I suggest that if we take note of that quotation we will exercise a greater degree of caution than is shown by some of those who support the motion now before the house.
We are told by the minister that we will have controls, and that these controls are foolproof. In other words we have nothing to worry about. The minister has great faith in the present West German government, but Adenauer will not be chancellor forever; and after Adenauer, what? These are questions that should be settled before we take the irrevocable step of placing arms in the hands of West Germans.
The German people are worried about this problem. I suggest that if they are worried about it, we also should be worried about it. Many in Germany and elsewhere fear that German rearmament at this time will lead to a West Germany dominated by the military. Such a government could take one of two steps to achieve the goal of reunification, both steps being unpalatable to the west. With an army, West Germany could seek by force of arms to achieve that which she has not been able to achieve by negotiation, namely the reunification of Germany. This could well provide the spark to set off a third world war.
The other course of action would be for a West German government to deal unilaterally with the Russians. It may be argued that these are possibilities rather than probabilities, but I believe the danger is there. I believe all hon. members should give serious consideration to the step they are being asked to take at this time. Are the 12 German divisions-which, of course, will be offset unquestionably by a similar build-up in the east-worth the terrific risks involved? That is a question which this house must answer.
In my view West German rearmament can be considered only in the light of two assumptions: first, that the efforts at German reunification be abandoned; or secondly, that reunification could be achieved by force. The first assumption is unacceptable. It is difficult to imagine that the German people will accept as permanent the division of their country into east and west. The second assumption is utterly unacceptable, since it involves a most serious threat to the peace of the world.
No one in this house has denied the risks and dangers involved in the rearmament of West Germany. The minister spoke of it

as a tragic necessity. I too consider it tragic, but I cannot agree that it is a necessity. The arguments advanced by the minister have not convinced me of the absolute necessity of taking this irrevocable step. I shall vote against this motion because in my judgment the dangers and risks involved far outweigh the possible advantages.

First of all, I cannot help agreeing with the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) and the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) that this government has failed to inform the people of all the circumstances which led up to our present position. In the present situation the public have not been fully aware of the fact that our "no alternative" position is the direct result of Russian communist unilateral action. Mr. Speaker, the proposed rearmament of Western Germany seems to upset and worry a great many of our fellow citizens.
As a matter of fact, if we were to take exclusively into account the history of Germany, the natural disposition of the German people to aggression and militarism, the atrocities and crimes committed by the Germans during the last war, then all that misgiving and worrying would surely be justified. However, I wonder whether it is fair to discuss that question only from the standpoint of Germany's past. I do not think it is. Since the last war, events have taken place that have deeply modified diplomatic relations between all nations, such as the creation of the United Nations Organization. Now less than ten years old, that organization has nevertheless marked a new chapter in the history of the world. Although we are generally inclined to look at the failings of UNO and to seldom consider its accomplishments, I think that some of these accomplishments will remain graven on the memories of men.
It should be mentioned here that in 1946, through a decision of its security council, UNO brought about the withdrawal of communist troops from certain provinces of Iran, at a time when their continued presence

North Atlantic Treaty would certainly have caused war. A few weeks later, through the work of the UNO security council, British and French forces were made to leave Lebanon, a move which prevented the outbreak of another war.
In 1947 the clash between Indonesia and The Netherlands was put to an end through negotiations and conciliation. We can add to that list the gradual pacification of the frontiers of Greece, the armistice in Palestine, the cease-fire in the struggle between India and Pakistan.
For the first time in the history of the world an international police force made up of soldiers from fifteen sovereign states fought under the United Nations flag against an enemy force which had just invaded Korea. It is also thanks to the United Nations that we have been able to bring hostilities to a close in that country. It would seem to me that these are important events that must be considered in examining the rearmament of Germany.
The setting up of NATO has been, in itself, a revolutionary undertaking in that it has banded together a group of European countries for the purpose of establishing collective defence and security, each country giving up a part of its sovereignty in order to contribute to mutual defence. That point, Mr. Speaker, is highly important with regard to this whole discussion.
Science has also contributed to changing the international scene. All of us will remember with what feelings we learned that it was the atomic bomb, in all its destructive power, which had put an end to the second world war. Since that time, we have been given the opportunity to ascertain the destructive force of the hydrogen bomb, which scared statesmen so, that nearly all leaders have exerted pressure to have the use of thermonuclear weapons prohibited.
Events moved on, so to speak, and at the suggestion of the president of the United States we saw the birth of an embryonic international atomic agency which nursed the hope of using thermonuclear energy for the welfare of the world rather than for its destruction.
You have no doubt heard about the progress made on the question of disarmament. Incidentally, on the question of disarmament, to those who seem to believe that Canada is assuming unjustified international prestige, I should like to point out that if there has been the slightest agreement on the question of disarmament, if there has been the least progress, it was due to the prestige, initiative and efforts of Canada in the United


Nations. I had the honour to be present when this matter was discussed. I had the opportunity of witnessing the efforts put forth and the work done by the leader of the Canadian delegation who was, at the time, the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I also realized that our country enjoyed in UNO and among all the nations of the world a measure of prestige which we do not even suspect here in Canada.
Everyone knows that we did not have to add to our military obligations; that did not cost the Canadian people one cent more. Besides we know that disarmament, if it could be achieved, would reduce not only international tension but also our foreign commitments and our national defence expenditures. As we all know, the amounts earmarked for the defence of our country make up more than half our budget. I cannot believe that we have come to the point where the government is criticized because Canada enjoys too great a prestige on the international plane.
However, Mr. Speaker, in view of all these happenings, we may say that our position is not the same as in 1914 or 1939. And what might not have seemed feasible at that time might be so today. For instance, I think we should now count on the rearmament of Germany on certain conditions.
All fears and worries that have been expressed about the rearmament of Germany have their source in two theories. In the first place, it has been said that, by giving arms to Germany, we are opening wide the gates leading to a new state of militarism that probably will bring about a third world war.
In the speech he delivered last week, the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) did not try to minimize the risks and dangers we were incurring. He gave us to understand that the very powers who proposed to rearm Germany recognized those dangers and deemed it necessary, in fact, to include in the protocol strict restrictions with respect to the quantity and the types of arms Germany would be allowed to keep. Moreover, the army in question, as we know, will be placed under the control of the NATO forces.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a matter of underestimating the dangers which may exist. There are dangers and we recognize them but on the

other hand we can be equally certain, morally certain, that every European nation, every member state of NATO, the United Nations themselves and, more particularly, France will watch closely for any tendency toward any expansion of the German army. If France, it seems to me, could ratify those agreements and accept the rearming of Germany, in spite of the sufferings imposed upon her thrice by Germany, we can be morally assured that every necessary precaution had been taken before approving the agreement.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) on the speech he made last week. It reflected profound and legitimate emotion, but it was also inspired by cold and calculated reasoning and logic. I am sure that the hon. member for Cartier is not enthusiastic about voting to rearm Germany, but that he will do so in the light of the present situation and as the lesser of two evils.
The second theory which has given rise to those misgivings is that, by rearming Germany, we will antagonize the Russians to the point that they might start a new world war. As for antagonizing the Russians, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the rearmament of Germany is going to antagonize them, but I am not ready to say that they will be antagonized to the point of starting a new world war. As a matter of fact, they have not made any important gain in the west European countries, because they fear the moral power of the European union and the military power of NATO.
It seems to me that it is our duty to bring more strength to that organization which, so far, has kept at bay the armed forces of the communists.
It must also be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that German rearmament and the integration of Germany into NATO is not only important, but absolutely necessary with regard to the establishment of adequate defences in western Europe. And it is precisely because Russia is afraid of this strengthening of NATO that, immediately following the London conference, she lost her head and sent out proposals and suggestions of all kinds, or invitations to conferences devoid of any meaning. It is for that very same reason too that Russia has contacted the communist party in Canada, enjoining it to exert pressure on every fellow-traveller group in this
North Atlantic Treaty
country, so that the federal government, and more particularly this parliament, would go on record as opposing German rearmament.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in the circumstances any attempt to diminish either the moral strength of the European union or the potential military strength of NATO would be a victory for Russian propaganda. And furthermore it is a notice, it is further evidence of the fiendish propensity of Russia to hide her hand so well, in the hope that the western powers be made to swallow gall for honey. We should not once again fall into this trap.
Besides, I sincerely believe that the true solution to this problem is much more important than the question of rearming Germany. This solution lies rather in the free nations giving the North Atlantic Treaty Organization all the support required to give it the strength and the effectiveness necessary to keep in check the communist threat of aggression on the one hand and, on the other hand, the necessary authority to be able to solve any problem likely to arise within the organization itself.
There will always be time, Mr. Speaker, to achieve universal disarmament once we have been given proof of the sincerity and good will of the communists.
If we cannot, Mr. Speaker, vote with enthusiasm for German rearmament, we should at least vote with determination and with confidence in the NATO forces which, since the beginning of the cold war, have held in check powerful communist forces in each one of the satellite countries of Russia.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we should have faith in NATO. Of course there are serious dangers in this whole question. We have to choose the lesser of the two dangers which we have to face. Those are facts and conditions which exist and which we cannot change, and this reminds me of this prayer of an English philosopher whose name I forget: Lord, give us enough serenity to accept the things which cannot be changed; enough strength to change the things which can be changed; and enough wisdom to differentiate between the two.
Mr. Speaker, after having considered for a long time this question of great import for the whole world, I intend to vote with confidence and without mental reservation for the rearming of Germany.

Mr. Speaker, tonight I am going to begin by begging the indulgence of the house to permit me to cite one or two experiences I had last fall. I think perhaps I am entitled to that indulgence because you will recall that last year I was the sole worker in this particular vineyard of debate, whereas this year there has been such a rush of workers that I have been almost squeezed out of the gate. So I am going to take a few minutes to tell of my experiences last year in Germany and in Berlin.
About four months ago I was in west Berlin, speaking to various people there, asking them about conditions in Berlin both east and west, asking about the way one might travel from the west sector to the east sector, speaking to such people as an old bookseller who told us about his quite hairraising experiences the year before when he had had to flee from east Berlin to save his life because he had resisted police pressure to allow his bookstore to be used as a point of control.
I had conversations with many people, in particular one lady who lived in Wannsee, whose son was a doctor, and whose practice took him into the east sector. She told us of her anxiety until her son arrived home each evening. I heard endless tales of almost unbelievable brutality and oppression in the east sector, tales which tragically were only too well authenticated.
With my wife I inquired about going from the west sector to the east sector, and we got conflicting answers. Some people held up their hands in horror at the very thought of anyone taking the unnecessary risk of going into the east zone. Others suggested that there was not any very great risk, that it was easy enough to accomplish.
We had gone to Berlin with the express purpose of seeing in east Berlin what we could of the communist regime. So one day we started down the Charlottenburgersallee to the Brandenburg gate, which is the division between the east and west zones of Berlin, a very interesting experience. Perhaps three or four cars went down that street while we walked the mile to the gate. Those cars were stopped, and the drivers and passengers put through a most careful and searching inquisition by the east German police. Even the few people who were on bicycles were stopped and were interrogated. But apparently, with the irrationality which
[Mr. Cardin.'J
often distinguishes totalitarian regimes, no one had suggested to them that they should ask questions of pedestrians.
So when my wife and I walked past the Soviet war memorial and through the Brandenburg gate, all that happened was that some rather puzzled and wondering glances were thrown in our direction by the armed German police. Nothing more was done. It was a most unpleasant sensation, however, to walk through the Brandenburg gate with these armed gentlemen behind us, wondering just what was going to happen.
We went through the gate to the Unter den Linden. We went into various establishments. We went there to find out what we could, and our first experience of what it is like to be in a police state occurred when we were standing in front of Humboldt University on the Unter den Linden. My wife was translating for me the notice on the board outside the university when I observed that a jeep had drawn up alongside the curb and a very unpleasant, young-looking man in uniform was gazing at us carefully and very searchingly. My wife went on translating. Out of the corner of my mouth I murmured, "The cops are here." She murmured back, "I know", then she took a deep breath, twirled around and stepped across the sidewalk in front of this man and asked him if we could go into the building, not having any idea what the building was.
Wherever we went we were confronted with that. We experienced the unpleasant sensation that there was always a man in uniform, someone watching us very carefully, and a most unpleasant experience it is. We had it even in a restaurant. It was a very eerie experience. It was a very good restaurant, good meals, not too expensive, crowded-and almost dead silence prevailed. It was a most unnerving and eerie experience to sit in a restaurant and hear only the occasional clatter of tools, and perhaps a murmured request for the salt. There was no conversation.
We went into the Karl Marx museum dedicated to that communist worthy. It was a very disheartening experience for a socialist, I may say, to see men, whose lives were devoted to a critical analysis of human society and, whether we agree with their methods or not, to the introduction of a better form of society, to see such people made into the objects of really idolatrous veneration. It was to me most repugnant and most unpleasant. In east Berlin there are obvious signs, to the most superficial observer, of a very unpleasant and evil state of oppression.

One can readily understand why those people in east Berlin in June of 1953 took their lives in their hands, as is set forth in this pamphlet that we got in west Berlin. There are pictures here of young men throwing brickbats at tanks, pictures of communists fleeing to the west sector. One can readily understand that after being in east Berlin. It was a very unpleasant experience, and certainly no one in his right senses would want to see such regimes spread their influence any further throughout the world.
But, Mr. Speaker, I had a question asked me repeatedly by Germans, both in Berlin and in other parts of West Germany. "What is your alternative to coming to some sort of terms with these people, short of war?" That question was asked of me repeatedly. The question is one I ask tonight. It is a question I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson); because if, as we were told the other day, the Canadian government is committed to wholehearted support of the view of the German people that German reunification must be the foundation of all policy with regard to Germany, then I have this question to ask. How do we propose, without war, to rescue those 18 million people from the communist regime which is now oppressing them, unless we are prepared to sit down and negotiate?
There is something intellectually dishonest in pretending or even implying that there may be some third alternative to negotiation or war; that there may be some way in which we can avoid having to negotiate with these people and thus remain on good terms with our United States friends, and at the same time avoid war and remain on good terms with our common sense and reason; but I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, there is no third alternative. We have only two prospects before us.
How do we propose to go about dealing with this great danger, this unpleasant situation? We propose to rearm a part of Germany in the face of widespread and growing dismay among the German people, and in the face of the often expressed fears of the Russians which, the Secretary of State for External Affairs admitted the other day, are understandable if possibly unreasonable fears.
What has been presented for approval in this house? When I was preparing notes for my speech, Mr. Speaker, I took occasion to check over some of the words of our Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I came to the conclusion that for one who formerly had at least some pretensions to being an historian, there were some remarkably shaky pieces of history in his argumentation. I was
North Atlantic Treaty
very interested tonight to note that the Ottawa Citizen is of the same opinion, and feels that poor history has had very rough handling at the hands of the Canadian parliament and no more rough handling than at the hands of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
As proof of the reckless and characteristic intransigence of our communist antagonists, we were told on Thursday last that the Berlin blockade was an example of the senseless, dangerous attitude of these people, and evidence of the folly of hoping to come to terms with them. I am quite prepared to agree that it was a senseless and dangerous procedure on the part of the Soviet authorities, but I do suggest that anyone wishing to present an historically true picture of the situation would have been obliged to mention the fact that that move, that senseless, dangerous move, wicked if you like, the blockade of Berlin was the direct result of an antecedent event. That event had been, of course, the expressed intention of the western powers to integrate the three western zones of Germany into one and to give it at least semi-sovereign status.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is indispensable to anyone who professes to present an historical review of circumstances to mention the whole chain of events. I am not arguing the merits or the demerits of the action taken at that time, but I do emphasize that one was the direct result of the other. It is dangerous folly for us to take actions of the communists that we dislike, examine them in isolation and overlook the antecedent events that led up to those actions.
We are told also that the Berlin conference of last year proved that an honourable and acceptable basis for agreement on German unity did not exist. I myself, Mr. Speaker, of course would hesitate to question the infallibility of our Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I would remind the house that a great many observers of the foreign scene of almost such stature came to a different conclusion. I would place on the record again the comments made in the London Observer, which is usually considered to be a fairly authoritative and objective journal, certainly not one that is tinged with communism or socialism. Speaking of the Berlin conference Sebastian Haffner, a very eminent observer, had this to say:
It would be rash for anyone to claim positively at this stage that Mr. Molotov's plan provides an acceptable form of that general "Locarno" or "mutual security" idea in Europe for which many western statesmen, from Sir Winston Churchill to Dr. Konrad Adenauer, the West German chancellor, have been groping during the last year, and which is indispensable-as has come to be widely recognized-if there is to be a general pacification of Europe. It would however be rasher still to deny

North Atlantic Treaty
the possibility that something on these lines might be developed from a patient and serious exploration of Mr. Molotov's proposal.
The eagerness with which the three western ministers in Berlin tried to sweep it off the table without consideration has been rather terrifying. It is undoubtedly one of the more intriguing proposals which have turned up since the war, and it should be the subject of careful study and diplomatic exchange, not only between the powers which were disputants at Berlin but among all interested European governments. It would be a great pity if the hastily contrived conference speeches and press comments of these hectic weeks were to be considered the last word on it.
Unfortunately that great pity came to pass. We all know that our Secretary of State for External Affairs occupies an eminent position in the world, but he has not hesitated to follow the rather rash course deplored by Sebastian Haffner. Just what did we do at Berlin? The suggestion is made that it was only the Soviet union who, shall we say, behaved in an intransigent manner. Just what proposal did we put to them? In essence the proposal was that the Russians should withdraw from East Germany, that they should agree to the unification of Germany on a basis which they and everyone else know meant adherence of that united Germany to the western bloc, and moreover there was to be an armed Germany.
Regardless altogether of our views of the communist world, regardless of our views of the Soviet regime, will anyone make the suggestion that that was a proposal we could reasonably expect them to accept? I could quote a great many competent non-communist observers who have suggested that Sir Anthony Eden's statements at that time were at least a little disingenuous, particularly when he suggested that the west was so generous that it did not mind to which bloc the newly united Germany would adhere. I suggest that if he did not mind to which bloc they adhered he had no business speaking for us. I suggest moreover that he knew perfectly well that if Germany were united because the western powers were able to bully or cajole the Soviet union into moving out of East Germany, naturally because of gratitude and self-interest they would move solidly into the western bloc. Let us face that fact frankly.
It has been pretended that it was a reasonable proposition. The fact that the Russian counter-proposal also contained some unacceptable jokers and some dishonesties, which it did, is no excuse whatever for pretending that our proposals were reasonable ones offered in the expectation that they would be accepted. I think we have the right to expect perhaps a more intelligent and adult conduct of our affairs in the face of this very dangerous and cunning adversary.

My colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) made reference to the latest Soviet note. I think it is rather significant that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not see fit to mention that the other day in his historical review. One might have thought he would have considered it relevant to this discussion. Whether it be good or bad, or acceptable or unacceptable, one can only presume that it is to be given the same unintelligent and cavalier treatment given to former suggestions.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested reasons why the Russians refused free elections last year. I think he is quite right in this. What happened in West Berlin was that the communists received only some 2-7 per cent of the vote. I was amazed that they got even that. But there was another conclusion to be drawn from this. While it is quite true, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs says, that the communists must have shuddered at the result of this, I suggest that Dr. Adenauer also must have had a few tremors because his party also went down to defeat. There was an indication in that West Berlin election that a reunited Germany meant the end of the Adenauer regime. I have no doubt that Willi Pieck would shudder. I expect that Konrad Adenauer had a shake to himself. So much for what I have termed the rather dubious historical foundation for the case put up by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I should like to say a word or two about the manner in which this case was presented. I wish I could agree with those who have complimented the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I really cannot. There was a time when responsible statesmen in dealing with foreign nations with which their country was presumably at peace observed a careful reserve and decorum in their statements. It was considered that until war broke out abuse was not very helpful, that it might indeed place obstacles in the way of reaching conclusions. Naturally the minute war broke out the lid was off.
I was somewhat dismayed, to be quite frank, at the tone of the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I had the feeling that instead of it being an adult, sophisticated, cold analysis of a dangerous situation which we had the right to expect, it was, on the other hand, a rather embarrassing combination of, what shall I say, hillbilly self-righteousness and disregard of the real actualities. It was an oversimplified way of presenting a very complex situation.

Let me quote what he said, as reported on page 362 of Hansard of January 20:
The communist dictators have already dragooned hundreds of millions of men- into highly centralized empires which deny the dignity and worth of the individual except as a creature of the state.
That may be factually true, although if by that he means that those hundreds of millions are struggling at the leash and waiting for the moment when we can release them, then I suggest it is a most dangerous delusion indeed. I would commend to the Secretary of State for External Affairs the words of a very eminent statesman spoken only last month in the city of Boston, which I should like to quote. They were as follows:
An arrogant Pharisaism and smug satisfaction with one's own superior righteousness, in a person or in a nation, are not only unamiable qualities, they are not conducive to clear political judgment. He whose humility and moral sensitivity is least highly developed, is most likely to confuse principle with question of fact or expediency, and to make an easy subconscious identification of his own viewpoint with the cause of right.
Furthermore, self-righteousness in international affairs is likely to lead to rigidity of thought and intolerance of other views. This often- prevents a wise understanding of complex and changing situations; and tends to make diplomacy captive and inflexible.
The author of those admirable words-and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will agree with me that they were wise and admirable words-was a gentleman by the name of Lester B. Pearson. But of course the Secretary of State for External Affairs was not addressing the Canadian House of Commons; he was addressing the assembly of the national council of the churches of Christ in the United States of America. Perhaps more important still, he was addressing them in the city of Boston, which has a well-deserved reputation of being allergic, shall I say, to the more illiterate forms of expression; of being allergic to oversimplifications and crudities of every sort.
I think it is to be regretted that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not considered the members of this House of Commons to be as worthy of that carefully considered and, if I may say so quite frankly, profound thinking that is expressed here, and instead saw fit to give us a sort of superman comic strip, a simplified and highly coloured statement about a very complex situation.

For example, I spoke to Mr. Artur Bratu, who is now superintendent of education in the state of Hesse. Mr. Bratu is a Jew who had to leave Germany during the Hitler regime but went back afterwards because he is also a German, and he considered he had a job to do in Germany.
Mr. Bratu was dismayed and distressed at the intentions of the western world. He said something of this sort to me. "We are now beginning to raise a new generation of young Germans with their faces turned against militarism. That is the only answer you have. I suggest it is very unwise for anyone in this chamber to be scornful of people like Mr. Bratu, who went back and put his head in the noose again because he felt it was his duty as a German to do so.
I had a talk with the member for Darmstadt in the Bundestag, Mr. Ludwig Metzger, who, like many of his colleagues, spent many years in and out of prison camps during the Hitler regime. He also expressed profound distress and uneasiness over the proposals now being made. I met another Jew, Heinz Putzrath, in Bonn, who had to leave Germany and go to England during the Hitler regime, where he was employed by the British government. He also went back to help build a new democratic Germany. He told me this. He said he himself was not so much concerned about the ex-nazis who were getting back into power-as they are doing in Bonn -as he was about the conditions that have been recreated in Germany by the western powers for the production of a new group of nazis. He said, "I find it difficult to have much confidence in a regime in which Alfred Krupp is again the dominant economic factor.

Then when it is again sought to add to Mr. Krupp a military arm, I am terrified at what may take place." One may well believe that he would be terrified. He was a Jew who had to get out. Most of his family died.
I had a long talk with Mr. Ollenhauer, leader of the social democrat party, who placed before me many of the arguments I have attempted to place before the house tonight. Mr. Ollenhauer also has an unimpeachable record of activity against the nazi regime, as have many of his colleagues in the social democrat party, such as people like Peter Blachstein who spent a year in Hitler's concentration camps and then escaped abroad; and Jacobi Werner, a man who spent seven years in Hitler's concentration camps. Now he is in the German Bundestag and is desperately afraid of the rearming of West Germany.
I could go on with an endless list of these people. Moreover, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that these are the people upon whom we have to rely if there is to be a democratic Germany arise, and that these are the people who tell us with one voice that we are insane to proceed with this project of rearming Germany at this time.
I do not know whether the clue to this situation is to be found in the statement with regard to United States policy which was made by our Secretary of State for External Affairs the other day, when he suggested that none of the alternatives was suitable or acceptable, particularly in the light of United States policy. Is that the milk in the coconut? Is that the real reason? Does that explain this determination to carry on in the face of a poor case in logic or, in fact, no case at all?
If so, Mr. Speaker, I can only express regret that our Secretary of State for External Affairs and our government did not follow the example of Pierre Mendes-France, the premier of France, who, when he laid the proposition before the French assembly, did not pretend it was a good thing but quite frankly admitted it was a bad thing and told them in effect, "This is it; this is the price of United States support; we have no option". If that is the situation, then we should be told frankly that it is.
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker-and neither is anyone else in this house-what will be the results of this move. I myself doubt that it will lead to war. I do not think so. I think the overriding danger of thermonuclear war will prevent that outcome. However, I think it may have disastrous effects for the very people in Germany who are our friends and allies, that it will place obstacles in the way of reunification of Germany in

Surely we all realize that it must be the goal of all our foreign policy and the goal of all international relations today to effect some sort of slackening of world tension so the human race can get about its overriding business of improving life for mankind on the face of the earth.
