Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) who has just spoken will not take it amiss if I say that the house, after so much brilliance, will consider my efforts to be pedestrian indeed.
I think every member who has spoken in this debate has referred to the importance of the question we are discussing and the difficulty of making a decision. The importance of the question before us is indicated by the seriousness with which almost every hon. member has approached it. I too feel that we are debating an extremely important question, and I hope that nothing I shall say will do anything to lower the high standard of the debate.
I wish to say at once that I am voting for the resolution. I am voting for it for reasons already stated by my leader, and perhaps for reasons which I shall put forward before I finish. I am also voting for the resolution because no acceptable alternative has been put forward by those who are opposing it. I say "acceptable alternative", although I think I could say equally well that no alternative has been proposed. I wish to say quite frankly that I have no alternative either.
The reasons for the ratification have been stated by a number of hon. members, including my leader. I shall try to avoid taking up the time of the house by repeating what they have already said. I shall, however, take a little time to try to analyse the arguments put forward by those who are opposed to ratification. I am in a most peculiar position this evening, Mr. Speaker, because my opposition, instead of being in front of me, to the left of me or to the right of me, is behind me. I think it is generally accepted that a person can do his best fighting when he can see the whites of the eyes of his opposition rather than when he feels their breath on the back of his neck.
I said I was going to analyse some of the arguments put forward by those who are opposing ratification of the agreements. What are those arguments? From a careful reading of the speeches that have been made I think they are as follows; First, that the arming

North Atlantic Treaty of Germany would widen the gulf between the democratic nations and the Soviet bloc. As one member speaking in opposition to the resolution said, it would push the division between the two camps "beyond the point of no return." Second, that the German people are not to be trusted; that Germany is still the Germany that twice in our lifetime has engulfed the world in war; that the Germany we would make a partner is the same Germany that was responsible for Dachau, Belsen and Buchenwald; or put more briefly, that the German people are not morally worthy to associate with the rest of us. Third, that the proposal to bring Germany into NATO- which we accept and which, of course involves the rearming of Germany-is premature and that another attempt should be made to negotiate with the Soviet union on the reunification of Germany. Fourth, that there is no enthusiasm in Canada for the ratification of the agreement.
I think these are the main arguments put forward by those who are opposing the resolution. I shall try to deal with the various points as they appear to me. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not approaching this matter lightly. I have gone over the various points made time and time again.
Let me deal with the first reason put forward for opposing ratification of these agreements. It was that the arming of Germany now would widen the gulf between the democratic nations and the Soviet bloc. When making this argument the speaker agreed that the west would have to negotiate from strength. If that is the case, what the speaker was really saying was that we must negotiate from strength but not from too much strength, that if the west becomes too strong the Soviet union will get cross with us and perhaps start something. The only logical conclusion I can draw from this position is that in the opinion of the speaker the west is strong enough now, and that any further addition to our strength must be opposed because it is likely to offend the Soviet bloc.
I cannot see the question in that way. I am quite satisfied that the only argument the people in the Kremlin understand is strength, and that the stronger we are the more likelihood there is of getting them to negotiate. Last year there were for the first time, I believe, in the history of the United Nations assembly, unanimous decisions on two issues. One was the resolution proposed by the United States with respect to atoms for peace, and the other was the resolution on disarmament initiated by the Canadian delegation. At the time the discussion and vote on the disarmament resolution were taking place, there were conferences in London and


Paris in an effort to bring about the agreements that we have been discussing for the last few days. It seems to me that if we show that we are strong enough the Soviet union, instead of refusing to negotiate, will be more reasonable and negotiate with us.
I want the house to understand that I am in favour of negotiation. The unanimous votes in the United Nations assembly this year must have been a really cheering sight. I was at the assembly in 1947 for a while as parliamentary adviser to the Canadian delegation, and I can assure hon. members that there was nothing more depressing than the fact that on every issue that arose the Soviet union was on one side and the western powers were on the other. Surely it must have been a heartening experience for those who were privileged to be at the last meeting to see unanimity achieved at least on those two points.
I come now to the second argument, that the German people are not to be trusted, that they are still the Germans who were responsible for Hitler's atrocities and consequently they are not fit to associate with us. That is an argument I cannot accept. I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) the other evening, that this is the master race doctrine in reverse. We may not be setting ourselves up as the master race, but we are certainly denouncing the Germans as a race of criminals.
I was-I hope you will excuse the word, but it is the kind of proletarian word you would expect from me-flabbergasted tonight to hear the statement that the Germans must wait until they have purged themselves of their national brutalities. If that is not setting ourselves up as something quite superior, I do not know what it is. But in any case I reject the idea of a criminal Germany with all the force of my being. I gave some years of my life to defending another people from the charge that they could not be trusted because of their race, and at this date I am not going to replace the Japanese with the Germans.
Let us admit that the Germans carry a very large share of the responsibility for starting two world wars. I have been walking around in this vale of tears for quite a long time- perhaps some people would say too long-and I remember some of the discussions that took place between the two world wars. The hon. member for Vancouver South will know quite well that most people with whom he and I associated at that time took the position that the Versailles treaty was responsible for Hitler, and that was the reason advanced by

many responsible people as to why Canada should not enter the second world war.
I think in the last few days we have overlooked altogether the part that Russia played in bringing about the second world war. Does anyone in this chamber tonight believe that if Stalin had refused to make an agreement with Hitler in 1939, Hitler would have marched on Poland? Of course he would not. If we are going to begin to apportion blame, if we are going to name criminal peoples, let us include them all.
However, let us agree that Germany must accept a very large share of the responsibility for starting two world wars. They have suffered for what they have done. I think I could say they have been punished for it. But it seems to me that if we want to give them an incentive for starting another world war the best way to do it is to ostracize them, to say to them that they are not fit to associate with other people, that they must be kept as a second-class nation. Let me repeat; if we want the Germans to start another world war, that, in my opinion, is the quickest way to get it started.
It also seems to me that those who are advocating such a course are overlooking the principles of modern psychology. In dealing with individuals guilty of crimes we have found that not only in their interests but also in the interests of society we must rehabilitate them as quickly as possible and bring them into association with other people. A sure way to have an individual guilty of an offence against society repeat that offence or another of its kind is to keep continually reminding him that he is different from other people because he once committed an offence.
I believe the same principle applies to peoples and nations. I think it is wrong to make every German responsible for the atrocities of the nazis. We know that hundreds of thousands of Germans refused to accept nazism. We know that thousands of them died because they refused. Thousands more rotted in concentration camps because they would not bow the knee to nazism.
As a matter of fact, a whole lot of people share the guilt for the rise of Hitler. I am going to read statements made by two prominent people, not communists, not socialists, not even Liberals, I believe. One of them was a former leader of the opposition in this house, the late Dr. Manion. Speaking in this chamber on the 8th of September, 1939, before war was declared by Canada, he said, as found at page 14 of Hansard:
One point I wish to make very clear is that to my mind we have no quarrel with the German people as a people. For generations they have given generously to the world in science and art and literature.
North Atlantic Treaty
We have well over half a million citizens of German descent in this country, and they are amongst our very best citizens.
And mark this one;
But, sir, Germany is controlled at the present time by an unscrupulous egoist. It is true he served Germany well, and had he stopped at a certain point he might well have gone down into history as a great German hero. He raised the German people from discouragement, gave them back their pride after a just but humiliating defeat. Had he stopped there he would have been accepted perhaps by all the world as a German hero.
That was after the Nuremberg decrees. That was after people all over Germany had been murdered by Hitler's minions. Now, Hitler could not have developed into the menace he became without assistance from other quarters. Let me read you another excerpt. The British people made great attempts to come to terms with Hitler. They sent an ambassador to Hitler in 1938, a man by the name of Sir Nevile Henderson, and his task was to bring about a working agreement between the United Kingdom and Germany. He failed. He wrote a book after he returned from Germany, when the second world war began, entitled "Failure of a Mission". This is a brief quotation from that book:
Nor are all dictatorships even if prolonged reprehensible. One cannot just because he is a dictator refuse to admit the great services which Signor Mussolini has rendered to Italy; nor would the world have failed to acclaim Hitler as a great German if he had known when and where to stop; if, for instance, after Munich and the Nuremberg decrees for the Jews.
It was an attitude like that of people who thought they were saving their possessions that gave Hitler his opportunity to nearly destroy the world. Now, let us not make other mistakes of that kind. What has taken place in West Germany in the development of democratic institutions since 1945 is, in my opinion, absolute proof that the people of West Germany, by a large majority, want to adhere to the democratic way of doing things. If we want to help them in that resolve we should welcome their co-operation and not spurn it. My own position is that West Germany should now be taken into the western comity of nations as a full partner, with all the privileges, responsibilities and obligations of full partnership.
Those opposing this resolution say they are not opposed to Germany regaining her sovereignty, or to bringing Germany into NATO, but only to the rearming of Germany. Now, I do not think it is possible to do the first two without doing the last. If we give Germany her sovereignty, then Germany is free to do whatever she likes. And I cannot imagine-and if what my hon. friends behind me

North Atlantic Treaty
say is true, they cannot imagine it either- a Germany that would be free to be a Germany that would not be armed.
I believe it has been said on many occasions that Germany will arm anyway. The question, I think, for us is, on whose side will she be after she is armed? Of necessity, in the kind of world in which we are living, she will have to And allies. Will she be absorbed into the iron curtain bloc, or will she be co-operating with the countries of the west who have helped her to organize her democratic institutions? That is the important question I think for us here in Canada, and for the whole democratic world.
Now for the third argument against ratification, that the proposal to bring Germany into NATO, which involves the rearming of Germany, is premature; that we should first make another attempt to negotiate with the Soviet union for the reunification of Germany. Let us see what such an attempt would involve. I am all for agreements through negotiation, if we can get what the trade unionists call negotiation in good faith. But I think it should be noted that Russia's interest in negotiation for the reunification of Germany has increased in direct proportion to the approach of the time when Germany would be actually brought into NATO.
However, it may be noted that the price the Soviet union demands to enter into such negotiation is that the proposal for associating Germany with the western powers should be dropped. I think that is important. In addition to that, as far as I know Russia has never agreed in clear-cut terms to free elections in Germany. But if the western powers would agree to the Soviet union conditions for negotiation on reunification-that is the throwing into discard of all attempts to bring Germany into NATO-have we any assurance that when that was done the Soviet union would negotiate in good faith? The result, to judge by our past experience, would be that the western powers, once they had done what the Russians wanted and once free elections were refused, would be thrown into confusion, and the Soviet union would be laughing up their sleeves at the ease with which they can confuse us.
The great obstacle to negotiation with the Soviet union is that the communists never negotiate or co-operate with others in good faith. We in the C.C.F. ought to know that. In the early years of our movement numerous attempts were made by the communists for joint action on community or national projects, for a united front, for co-operation on this and that. But we always found that the communists would never stick to their agreement. Even when they called meetings to
[Mr. Maclnnis.f
denounce nazism and fascism, as was the case before the Stalin-Hitler pact, and brought well-intentioned groups from various walks of life to take part in such meetings, they always injected a resolution or a speaker or something else that was not provided for in the arrangements, all designed to give them control of the situation. The result has been- I may say the result has been good so far as we are concerned-that in the last 15 years, ever since the beginning of world war II, the C.C.F. has refused to associate with them in any way, at any time, in any place, on any issue.
The experience of the trade union movement has been the same. Not so many years ago I heard prominent officials in the two large labour congresses say they would never allow a man's politics to determine his right to belong to a trade union, or to be an officer of a trade union. But because of the disruptive activities of the communists in the trade union movement these congresses had to change that resolve. They had to throw the communists out. That was the only alternative to having the unions torn to pieces. It is no different in international affairs.
I remember many years ago reading a book by Bruce Lockhart, who was in the Soviet union at the time of the revolution. He was there as a very young man, in the British foreign office, and I think he spent some time in jail there. In his book "British Agent" he tells the story about Karl Radek, one of the old bolsheviks preparing to go to a conference with the mensheviks. It must have been early in the revolution, because the mensheviks were liquidated shortly after.
Mr. Radek, preparing his speeches in reply to the decision taken by the mensheviks, prepared one speech in case they took position A. He prepared another speech in case they took position B. He put the argument for position A in one of his coat pockets, and he put the argument for position B in the other. He was in a great flutter for a while after reaching the conference room because he had forgotten in which pocket was which speech.
The tactics of the communist party- whether in Vancouver, Regina, Toronto or Moscow-have not changed in the slightest degree since Radek's time.
I believe in negotiation. To negotiate on every problem that cannot be settled otherwise is a part of my philosophy of life. But in negotiation we should be very careful not to give away an advantage that we now have until we are pretty sure that we are getting value in return. In other words, in any negotiations on the unification of Germany we should be sure that the soviets will agree

to free elections in Germany. They have never, let me say again, to my knowledge made a categorical statement that they will agree to free elections under United Nations supervision.
Now for my fourth and last point, having to do with the argument that we should oppose this motion because there is no enthusiasm in Canada for the ratification of the agreements. I am going to overlook the fact that I think "enthusiasm" is the wrong word, but who am I to take issue on the meaning of a word with my colleagues who are university graduates? I quite agree there is no enthusiasm for ratification of these agreements. I think it could be equally well said that there was no enthusiasm for the North Atlantic treaty when it was ratified, or for entering the second world war, for that matter. But there was something else. There was determination, and that is the word we want here. We had on those occasions something to preserve, our freedom, our democratic institutions. What was happening in the world was endangering our freedom; there was a job to be done and, much as we disliked it, we did our part, if not with enthusiasm, with steady determination. We are in the same position today. If there is not enthusiasm for the ratification of the agreements, there is certainly no enthusiasm on the part of the people opposing them; that is, if you leave the labour progressive party and its fellow travellers out of the picture.
Some hon. members have referred to the delegations that interviewed them, when those people were in Ottawa a few weeks ago. None of them came to see me but I have had some letters. I have received 34 letters, 8 telegrams and 6 petitions such as those the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) mentioned in the directive, issued by the labour progressive party. Nearly all these letters, telegrams, and communications came from communist sources. There are two or three letters the writers of which I have not been able to classify. Outside of these I have not received a single communication from a responsible individual or organization, either trade union, board of trade, veterans' organization or any other organization opposing the ratification of the agreements.
Speaking for myself, as I said before I am going to vote for the resolution before us because I believe it is a step to prevent war rather than to make war. Socialist parties in the NATO countries in Europe, which are much closer to Germany than we are and who have in the past felt the full effects of German aggression, have already ratified these agreements. They have done so because they felt the only way to prevent aggression was to be strong.
North Atlantic Treaty
Everyone regrets the necessity of rearming Germany. I can say with equal truth that everyone regrets the necessity of any armaments, that is anyone with any sense. But as I said before, Germany will be rearmed in any case. The question then is, on whose side is she going to be? I want her to be on our side; consequently, voting on this issue as a Canadian and as one who is anxious above everything else to support every move toward world peace, I am going to support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Earl Rowe (Acting Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), and it was very encouraging to hear the soundness of his logic. This is an issue that is of solemn concern to everyone in this house and to thousands and thousands throughout the country who are stirred at times, as has been so well said, by emotion and sentiments born of days that are gone. One can look back over 40 years of turmoil in this country, filled with tragic realities of hot wars and cold wars and constant anxiety. These years have given us experience and education and I hope foresight enough to meet the future as stronger and more intelligent people, and better informed than we were before the first great war.
The dearth of information that was given to the house and the country prior to these international difficulties has been all too conspicuous. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, as we were approaching the second world war it seemed to me we never did use the experience we had or the information that was available to us to face the realities as we should. I am not going to review past events because this is not the time, when we are dealing with this solemn issue.
There is not an hon. member here who was present at that time who does not understand what I mean. In 1937 we were told that there was no danger of war with Germany. We were told by our prime minister at that time, who had visited Germany and talked with Hitler, that there was no danger of war at all. Then in 1938, when great preparations might have been made in this country in close co-operation with the old land, we were still told there was not much danger. Steps could have been taken then, Mr. Speaker. They were not taken. And what a price we paid for neglecting to face reality!
However, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to find that since these years have passed and our experience has been ripened by the hard, cold and bitter penalties for neglect, you might say, we are no longer faced with political

North Atlantic Treaty
fears at home which becloud the glaring and tragic realities abroad. We meet tonight, Mr. Speaker, and I am proud of the fact that the two historic parties in this dominion stand foursquare with their chins to the wind, as the saying is. Differences of class, race, creed, religion or party have not separated us in our determination, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings way (Mr. Mac-Innis) has said, that if it is within our power we shall spend the last vestige of energy we have to avoid another awful war. We must as a parliament, as Canadians, lead the way. I do not mean lead the way in world affairs so much, but lead the way in this country. We dare not mislead.
Following the first great war it will be remembered that we were told we were going to have no more war, that the old league of nations was going to solve our troubles. Then after the second world war we were told that the United Nations would save us from any such recurrence. Then we embarked on the Atlantic community pact. After each in its turn seemed to be inadequate we were sure that we had found the answer to at least a greater degree of security in EDC, which I believe was signed in Paris in 1952.
The French premier, Mendes-France, called the EDC partners together in Brussels in August, 1954 and tried to get the agreement amended so as to make it more acceptable to the French parliament. Mendes-France failed in this and the French parliament refused to ratify that agreement, and it fell through for the time being.
Again we were happy to find that the traditional British leadership, which has so often been like a beacon light in the world's darkest hours, led the way to new hope. The Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden offered to keep the British ground forces and the Royal Air Force in Europe for 44 years. That must have convinced France as well as all our other allies among the free peoples of the west that Great Britain was facing up to realities no matter what the cost might be. No one has intimated that any one country can stand alone as an independent vacuum in the heart of Europe.
I am endeavouring as best as I can not to take up the time of this house unnecessarily by repeating speeches which have been made already, some more from emotion than logic, and with little effect upon this issue. But I do think we should review the steps that were taken, and know exactly what is before this house.
I have mentioned EDC; I have mentioned its collapse; I have mentioned

how the great British foreign secretary, Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden, representing that greatest of all world statesmen today, Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill, led the way as that country has done so often in the past. We had the London meeting at which a new Brussels treaty was agreed upon. Remember that we were not there. The parties to that treaty were France, the Benelux countries including Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, Great Britain, West Germany and Italy. This agreement which was signed in Paris on October 23 provided for the association of West Germany with Europe, making Great Britain a party to the arrangement and in fact settling West Germany's rearmament there and then.
The minister for external affairs made a very lucid speech on Thursday last. If some hon. members were not listening as closely as they should have been, if they read his speech again they will see that he explained that the sovereignty of West Germany was settled. We are not settling the sovereign rights of Germany tonight; we are not settling the rearming of Germany. We are deciding whether she shall be included in NATO. The aims and terms and safeguards of the agreement have been elaborately and sincerely expressed in this debate by the minister for external affairs and by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who made a splendid speech the other night on behalf of this party. The minister for external affairs presented a broad picture of the problem, and the hon. member for Prince Albert expressed our position most fluently.
We have made our choice as a party. We are going to support this resolution, confident that there is no other common-sense or available alternative at this time. In listening to the speeches made by my socialist friends to my left, the majority of whom appear to have made up their minds to vote against this resolution, I am at a loss to understand the basis of their cloudy and fantastic reasoning.
Let us suppose for a moment that my socialist friends had their way and West Germany's admission to NATO was refused. Stop and think what that would mean. In this matter as in many others they know they have no hope of having to assume responsibility. There are those of us who still hope to have responsibility in this country. I do not for one moment doubt their sincerity, but let us suppose again that their arguments are accepted and we are not going to allow West Germany to be included in NATO. What would be the obvious reality then?
West Germany is already admitted to the western European union. West Germany is

already recognized as a sovereign power. West Germany's right to arm is already established. Let us strip oft the cloak of unreality from this solemn issue. Let us look at what it means. We are still one of the 14 member countries of NATO. Our responsibility for the defence of the North Atlantic community still stands unaltered by any such rejection as my hon. friends now suggest. It is not to be changed by that. You would have six nations of the North Atlantic community and the republic of West Germany in one pact, while under the new Brussels treaty all six except Germany would be members of NATO. Our responsibilities would be in no way lessened; they would be still clearly defined under NATO, and our influence would be embarrassingly impaired by such utter nonsense.
The members of the socialist party to my left have expressed keen concern about the rearming of Germany, to which agreement our country was not a party. They now propose to forfeit any right to fix the terms and conditions upon which that country shall proceed with the armament program already established. Stop and think of it. They are loud in their opposition and protest against the rearming, but they propose to relinquish the only opportunity we would have for any control, supervision or direction of how they would use those armaments. I have listened very carefully to the speeches during this debate, because lately with my new responsibilities I have sat in the house more diligently than has been my habit in the past.

Do not applaud too much, because if I did not have to I would not endure you hon. members opposite as much as I already have. But as I said, I listened carefully to the strange doctrine vigorously expressed by socialist members during this debate, and I heard their loud protests about rearmament despite the fact that we have little alternative in this matter. They refuse to accept the efficacy of the controls and supervision included in this agreement, and when I hear that I wonder what is happening.
I am amazed and shocked at such folly in reasoning. I do not wish to question their sincerity for one moment, but I would not dare suggest that their reasoning should be accepted. When I hear of the visit of Mr. Attlee to this country I think I might be pardoned if I suggest to my socialist friends that they arrange another visit for the Hon. Mr. Bevan, who has taken a similar position in the United Kingdom, so that at least half
North Atlantic Treaty
or a majority of the socialist members in this house can take the journey across Canada with him.
Who would dare say that if West Germany were refused admittance to NATO she would venture to stand alone? I believe she would be compelled to face realities in the same manner as other nations in these days. There would be only one other choice for her, and that other choice could only be toward those who would like to see her refused admittance.
To my mind the question is quite clear-cut, and it worries me when I hear that some hon. members in this house indicate their intention to register a vote against this resolution. I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house, but I hope I have said as much in a short time as some hon. members with emotional speeches have said over a longer time.
But, Mr. Speaker, I would not feel I was doing my duty if I did not underline the danger involved in this step, without indulging in emotional rhetoric. There is little need for me to review these dangers, for I see before me men who have fought in two great wars. I have heard them make speeches that would move the coldest heart and the most stolid temperament in this house. It has not been my practice to seek the indulgence of this house in order to read articles or quote the views of others because I know it is not recognized by you, Mr. Speaker, as good parliamentary practice, and in that you have my full agreement. Mr. Speaker, I am not sure I have full unanimity, but I am positive that I have a majority. As I said, I feel this issue far transcends party politics, and in the regrettable absence of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) for whom I am acting as substitute, I would like to read a brief extract expressing his views, which was written before this issue came before the house. The article was written on October 16, 1954, and concerned the question of admitting Germany into the western community of free nations. It outlines his views on this issue as follows:
When I returned to Paris from Berlin the Arc de Triomphe reminded me very vividly that Wellington and his associates were confronted with somewhat the same problem after the Napoleonic wars nearly 140 years ago.
Wellington reduced the problem to a very simple proposition. He said that if they were prepared to remove from France every Frenchman and resettle the country with other people, then this idea might make sense. But if they believed that France was going to be populated by French people, then their purpose must be to try to bring France into full fellowship with the other nations of Europe. His views prevailed and as a result of that decision one of the greatest historic friendships of all history was established between France and Britain after centuries of almost continuous war.
There are always such developments in the history of human progress. Hope springs eternal in the human breast, and all humanity must overcome emotional prejudices and bitter traditional sentiment born of days that are gone.
We can face the future with justifiable hope if we have a steadfast faith in the co-operative efforts of all who wish to be free. We must stand up and be counted. We must not turn back. We must face the issue. There is nothing so fearful as fear. But under the eternal vigilance and co-operation of free men of the western world, I do not believe we need to be afraid. If we are strong enough, honest enough and bold enough to meet as we should these respective issues as they arise, I believe not only can we avoid a third world war but can achieve the lasting hope of all, namely that we may have peace in our time.
